items.sum: C. R. Woodard's summary of his Belgrave Hall talks on athletic injuries, urging athletes to see a specialist at once and advising on muscle tears, sprains, foot fractures, bruised soles and torn knee cartilage.
items.s: ATHLETIC INJURIES C. R. Woodard's summary of his Belgrave Hall talks on athletic injuries, urging athletes to see a specialist at once and advising on muscle tears, sprains, foot fractures, bruised soles and torn knee cartilage. ATHLETIC INJURIES By C. R. WOODARD, Accident Officer, The Middlesex Hospital, W.1 I have been asked to write a summary of the talks on athletic injuries that I gave last winter in Belgrave Hall. Although there was a very poor attendance, I know that all athletes are justifiably worried as to what they should do to get the best advice if they are unfortunate enough to sustain injury, and the purpose of this article is not only to make this clear, but to point out some of the risks that are taken if such injuries are neglected. Firstly, it is essential to see a specialist at once, unless, of course, you prefer to spend months of doubt as to how severe the injury is. In a great hospital such as my own there are facilities for investigating such injuries, and no doubt is left as to the type or severity of them. If you appreciated how easily and how often mistakes are made, you would never rely on anybody but an expert; wrong treatment not only leads to months of delay, but may mean you never take an active part in athletics again. This hospital, for one, is open night and day and is always prepared to see anyone. After five o'clock in the evening it is not possible to make any specialised investigations, however. British athletes are renowned for their blind trust in unqualified “ quacks.” They do not realise that, for every success, such a man has a hundred failures. We see them in places like this, and if any of you had seen one in a hundred of other people's mistakes that we have seen in the last six months, you would be appalled. I do not say that we make no mistakes, but we have heaps of facilities to reduce our mistakes to an absolute minimum. There are certain principles of treatment of athletic injuries and, although as I have said previously, you must see a specialist at once, no matter how trivial the injury, the first-aid treatment of many common injuries is vitally important. The bugbear of athletic injuries is rest. The old idea of resting strains and partial tears of muscles is wrong. They must be exercised at once. The guiding principle is not rest, but work. A well-known athlete, 12 months ago, pulled a muscle in his thigh and was told to rest. He was unable to run again that season as a result of this advice because his muscles went so stiff. He was getting back into training for this season, when he tore it again. I immediately treated him and got him back on the track within two hours, running perfectly. He has since won several races and suffers no recurrence of the trouble. That demonstrates how different the results of the right treatment can be from the wrong. I might add that a full report of this case is being given to the official medical journals, because the treatment is revolutionary and promises to be outstandingly successful. The principle of rest for such injuries is wrong, for rest leads to fibrosis and contractions; the muscle tone is lost. Whereas active exercise enables the rest of the affected muscle to take over, and the increased circulation removes the swelling and bruising caused by the tear. All sprains, whether of ankles, knees or wrists, should be strapped at once and actively used. In the case of ankles, the strapping should extend from toes to below knee and completely cover the heel. Then only a minimum amount of swelling occurs. There should be no massage for at least a week. There are two other athletic injuries which are often wrongly treated and misdiagnosed. Firstly, the broken bone in the foot. This is a far commoner injury than people suppose. In the cold spell at the beginning of this year, while training over the country, not racing, at least six well-known athletes, including two internationals, broke bones in their feet. If treated correctly there is no reason why any one of these men shouldn't be back to form within two months. Treated wrongly, with failure to realise that the bone is broken, and only X-ray can confirm this, the athlete may never run again. But six such cases have been seen by us. I wonder how many more there were, and how many still remain unrecognised. The other common injury that I want to mention is bruising of the sole of the foot, due to hard ground and tracks. An athlete may find the soles of his feet painful for months on end. It is simply due to bruising, and can be immediately relieved by wearing spongy rubber soles, in both ordinary shoes and running shoes. No harm can be done by drawing attention to other types of injury. Everyone has heard of a torn cartilage of the knee. There are not more than a handful of surgeons in this country who could make a certain diagnosis of this injury in any case and get it right every time. And yet most sportsmen and athletes, if they sustain a torn cartilage, or other injury of the knee, allow their knees to be massaged and manipulated by a masseur! He can never be certain to any degree whatsoever of what he is dealing with, and often has never even heard of a torn cartilage, torn ligaments, loose ligaments, or loose bodies, just to mention four conditions which may occur in the knee, and all of which require different treatment. He remains unaware of the enormous harm he can do to the knee if he encourages a man to go on playing or running with a torn cartilage in the knee. A torn cartilage has to come out, and only a surgeon can take it out. A torn ligament, on the other hand, responds to non-surgical treatment, but why be in any doubt as to which injury you have sustained? Some people have sustained a torn cartilage in the knee, gone on using it, set up an arthritis in the knee, and for the rest of their lives had trouble with it. All this because they never saw a surgeon, who could have told them at the first that they must have it out. Recently a first-class athlete tore his cartilage, playing rugby football. It was taken out, and within three months he won the two sprints in an inter-university meeting. He is an Olympic hope. There is no reason to suppose he will have any further trouble with his knee. If he had not received expert advice he might still be doing the knee harm by trying to play with the torn cartilage. Many first-class athletes have done so in the past and have ruined themselves. I had hoped by now to have started an advisory clinic for athletes after working hours in the evenings, but I have met a great deal of opposition from old buffins all the way along the line, so I cannot yet say the idea has materialised. However, perhaps it will have done so by the time you see this. But if you want advice, and at the same time realise how you are helping to collect data and knowledge on such injuries, come and see us at this hospital, and we will give you all the help we can. C. R. Woodard C. R. WOODARD Accident Officer, The Middlesex Hospital, W.1; gave talks on athletic injuries at Belgrave Hall last winter C. R. WOODARD The Middlesex Hospital Belgrave Hall

items.sum: Editorial on the club's healthy start to Olympic Year 1948, with nine members named official Olympic Possibles, the value of club racing, and belated New Year greetings.
items.s: Editorial Editorial on the club's healthy start to Olympic Year 1948, with nine members named official Olympic Possibles, the value of club racing, and belated New Year greetings. The Club has begun 1948 in good fettle. The numbers of active Walkers and Runners turning out each week are pleasing to behold and we need have no fear that we are not a flourishing Club. This year being Olympic Year, is an important one for all Athletes. We have nine official Olympic Possibles in all Athletic events, the third largest number from any club, only Achilles and Polytechnic have more. We are proud of this selection and our best wishes go out to these members. It must not be forgotten that besides these members there are one or two others who must be considered as unofficial possibles and who might spring something of a surprise on the Selectors. We hope they do! For those of us who are not of Olympic standard there are the usual Club races, over the Country or Road and on the Track, to support with our wholehearted efforts. The Popular Press, which normally takes so little interest in Athletics, will undoubtedly create its own Olympic legends and stories; most of this will only be concerned with individuals and how fast they can move or throw. It will be most unlikely that the sheer sportsmanship of losing, as well as of winning, will come into any of this, for such things can only be properly understood by the man who has played the game in the hard and clean school of English Club Athletics. We know that it is from these that our champions grow and our spirit springs with such fertility. To represent one's Country is a matter of some pride, but the running of a good race for the honour of one's Club can also give one claim to a measure of modest pride in something well done. No true Belgravian can afford to forget this. * * * * * Our last issue came too early for us to include Christmas Greetings to all members and friends. This issue arrives a little late for New Year Greetings but, nevertheless: To All Our Members and Friends A VERY HAPPY AND PROSPEROUS NEW YEAR. Olympic Games Achilles Polytechnic

items.s: Obituary Obituary of Past President A. F. W. Macher, who died on 13 November 1947 and had presented the club's 10 Miles Cross Country Championship Shield. We regret to announce the death of Past President A. F. W. Macher, on November 13th, 1947. Our sympathy goes out to his sons Albert (a former Club Hon. Treasurer) and Gus Macher, and other members of his family on their great loss. The late Mr. Macher presented our 10 Miles Cross Country Championship Shield for competition many years ago and there can be little doubt that this gift served to emphasise the importance of running the full Cross Country Championship distance of 10 miles within the Club and laid the foundations of later Southern and National sucesses. We mourn his passing. A. F. W. Macher A. F. W. Macher Past President; died 13 November 1947; presented the club's 10 Miles Cross Country Championship Shield Albert Macher Albert son of A. F. W. items.sum: Report of the club's Annual General Meeting at Belgrave Hall on 11 October 1947: reports, rule changes, Life Memberships and election of officers.
items.s: The Annual General Meeting Report of the club's Annual General Meeting at Belgrave Hall on 11 October 1947: reports, rule changes, Life Memberships and election of officers. BELGRAVE HALL SATURDAY, 11th OCTOBER, 1947 There was a muster of over ninety, representing all sections of the Club, for this very important meeting. Our President, Harry Parker, was in the chair, and it was most pleasing to see many Past Presidents amongst us. The Hon. Secretary, Alf. Harley, read the notice convening the meeting, and then the Minutes of the last A.G.M., which were confirmed. The Hon. Secretary's report was adopted without it being read to the meeting, as it had been included in the notice of the meeting sent to members. He thanked the many Club officers and members for their loyal and unselfish help throughout the year, and announced that the Committee had decided to award the T. W. Green Trophy (for the best athlete of the year) to Harry Churcher. The Hon. Treasurer, Bill Webb, then presented the Accounts and Balance Sheet. The expenses of a Club of our size are no small matter, especially in view of rising costs etc., but thanks to the heartening amount of subscriptions and donations he was able to give us an encouraging picture of our finances. Once again he praised and thanked Les. Cohen for his work in connection with the Supporters' Club, and paid tribute to the help given him by the Assistant Hon. Treasurer, Tommy Morrell, and by the Hon. Auditors. The report was adopted. The next item was the alteration of some of the Club Rules. The Rules had been carefully examined by a special sub-committee and their reccommendations were explained by the Hon. Secretary. He said that the proposed alterations were in the nature of a tidying up of the rules, which, incidentally, were drawn up in the Club's early days, when conditions were different. The proposed alterations were agreed to with two amendments, viz.: Rule 7, the proposal (new Rule 7c) requiring a quorum of twenty-five members for an A.G.M. was rejected. New Rule 11 was amended so as to include any new member from a distant club, who had qualified to represent us under the A.A.A. Hard Cases Rule, as eligible to compete in Club Championships. The Committee's nominations for Life Membership were then considered. Joe Coleman, proposed by Syd. Roberts and Cyril Pateman, and Tommy Morrell, proposed by Harry Shields and Arthur Penny, were duly elected to this great honour. Both of these popular members have put in many years of hard work for the Club and have been loyal team men. Both made short speeches of thanks. Then to the Election of Club Officers. Alf. Harley proposed that Harry Parker be re-elected Club President. This was seconded and the meeting approved with acclamation. The Vice-Presidents were re-elected en bloc with the addition of Dr. Christopher Woodward and Len. Rollins. The former, as our Hon. Medical Adviser, needs little introduction, and in a few words of thanks reiterated the importance of prompt and proper treatment for injuries, Len. Rollins's election will give much pleasure to his many old friends in the Club, he was a great club man in pre-war days, and is now “ mine host ” in South Kenkington. There were few changes in the other Officers. Alf. Taylor takes over as Cross-Country Captain. How many of our younger members know that Alf. was in our first winning teams in the Southern (1934) and English (1935) Cross-Country Championships? He will be supported by Arthur Penny, triple Cross-Country International, British Empire Six Miles Champion (1934), etc., and Bert Smith, another who has been running for years, and is still improving, as Vice-Captains. Our Road Walking Captain, Charlie Churcher, will have Jack Bidgood, who has made a welcome reappearance on the road, and Joe Wilson, one of our coming long-distance men, to help him. Our Track Walking Captain, Joe Coleman, recommended that Harry Churcher be elected to this office for 1948, Olympic Games Year. This was carried and Joe was elected Vice-Captain. Charlie Jones, who has been Field Events Secretary and Captain stood down from the latter post, to which another member of several year's standing, Bill Sutton, was elected, with Geoff. Freestone as Vice-Captain. Harry Shields was re-elected Track Captain and will be helped by Frank Simmons and Jim Beaumont. One or two matters were raised under Any Other Business, and these will have the attention of the new Committee. The Meeting closed with a vote of thank to the Chair. G.S.D. items.h: The Diamond Jubilee Dinner and Dance
items.sum: Report of the club's Diamond Jubilee Dinner and Dance at the Duke of York's Headquarters, Chelsea, on 25 October 1947, chiefly the speeches.
e: Belgrave Harriers Diamond Jubilee Dinner and Dance
items.s: The Diamond Jubilee Dinner and Dance Report of the club's Diamond Jubilee Dinner and Dance at the Duke of York's Headquarters, Chelsea, on 25 October 1947, chiefly the speeches. SATURDAY, 25th OCTOBER, 1947 DUKE OF YORK'S HEADQUARTERS, SLOANE SQUARE, CHELSEA This important occasion was very well supported by our members and their many friends. We all enjoyed the Dinner, we all enjoyed the Drinking and the Dancing, but the most interesting part of the evening was the speeches. These were begun by the President, who proposed the Health of The King and then of the Club. He was followed by our Hon. Secretary, who made a fine speech of thanks to the President and went on to speak of the well known Club spirit. He mentioned how successful we had been in fostering all branches of our sport and of our friendships with other clubs. He finished by saying how he was sure our success was not in the nature of a cycle of success, but that we should continue leading and fostering the sport of Athletics. The speech of the evening was made by one of our new Vice-Presidents, Doctor C. Woodard, who proposed the health of our Guests. Dr. Woodard said that in his opinion British Athletics faced near disaster in 1948, through lack of proper food and either wrong attention or no attention of athletical injuries, from which so many of our Olympic prospects suffer. He stressed his points with considerable skill and force, and obviously his audience were behind him and listening with rapt attention. He went on to accuse the Athletic Officials of dilatoriness in obtaining food parcels from the Empire for Olympic possibles. When he resumed his seat the applause was very warm and continued for some time. Mr. Jack Crump, who was one of the guests, replied to Doctor Woodard's accusations. He thought that the Doctor had exaggerated the state of things and that our Athletes were being looked after better than ever before. Food parcels would be coming in plenty and they had been obtained as early as was possible. Mr. Crump finished by appealing to the Clubs to help our Olympic prospects, he felt sure they would. The speeches finished with a nice tribute to our President by the Hon. Treasurer, to which the President replied with all modesty. Our thanks must go to the Hon Social Secretary for organising such a grand evening under the most trying and difficult circumstances. We all enjoyed ourselves and will remember the Belgrave Diamond Jubilee Dinner for a long time. C. Woodard Doctor C. items.s: Commentary Club news column: a planned reprint of Jimmy Belchamber's portrait of Bob Ricketts, use of headquarters by other bodies, a new Club Marathon Championship, members' news, the International Cross Country Championship at Reading, the South of Thames Junior race, county representatives in the Inter County C.C. Championship and the walkers' open-race record. It is proposed to include in our next issue Jimmy Belchamber's portrait of Bob Ricketts, which was published in the Belgrave News Letter, last April. This article, on one of our finest members, is well worth reprinting for it is a classic of its kind. Our Wimbledon Headquarters have been placed at the disposal of, Mount Pleasant (G.P.O.) Sports Club, Wandsworth, Putney and Barnes Scouts, and London Business Houses S. and S.A., for the running of their championships. Similar hospitality will be extended to Surrey County A.A.A., County of London Cadet Sports Council and London Rover Scouts Association, during the weeks to come. This is just another way in which our Club helps Athletics along. Allan Sexton represented the South of England against the North in the Schoolboys' Rugger International at Roslyn Park on 23rd December, 1947. Our congratulations Allan. A Club Marathon Championship, under normal Club Championship conditions, has been instituted and will be contested for the first time this year. It will be held in conjunction with the Polytechnic Marathon on June 19th, which this year will also embrace the A.A.A. Championship. No Club Trophy, as yet, exists for this our latest Championship, but in the fulness of time it is hoped that a generous donor will help to provide a trophy worthy of this Club event, for perpetual competition. Congratulations to Past President Oscar Horwood on his recent marriage, our best wishes are extended to him. It is very interesting to hear that Past President Teddy Gordon was elected Deputy Mayor of Malden and Coombe, with Mrs. Gordon as Deputy Mayoress. Ted retired from business worries at Christmas and now intends to spend all his leisure time in civic duties. Our best wishes go to him. Our President writes to remind me that little publicity has been given by the Club to the most important Cross Country event for many years in Southern England. He refers to the International Cross Country Championship to be run at Reading on April 3rd. One of our members, Wally Jewel, has been elected President of the Meeting and a special request has been made by the Southern Counties C.C.A. that all Southern Clubs endeavour to support this fixture. The Hon. Social Secretary is running a coach to this function, details will be announced later. Members are reminded that to keep the Club address book up to date any changes of address should be notified to the Hon. Secretary. This does not apply to members in the Forces. Running over a very hard five miles course, our “ A ” Team finished second in the South of Thames “ Junior ” Championship, held at Dartford in Kent. As we had won this race the two previous years we have every reason to feel proud with this year's effort. The best running was that of two of our under twenty-ones, Eddie Short and Mike Heard who finished fourth and twelfth respectively. Harry Churcher is back on the Road again and so far unbeaten this year, although pulled out of the “ Belgrave Open.” Perhaps it is because we think he wins quite enough anyway! He was pulled in the same race last year. That incredible old-timer Bert East is still walking better than ever and improving with every race. His latest effort is to beat Rutland, McMullen and Coleman in the Club 10. Bert is the Handicappers Headache, how they must love him! That well known Club, Cadogan A.C., were third in the Middlesex C.C. Championship. Vic. Blowfield, second, and Tommy Clinton, fifth, ran exceptionally well and were both chosen for Middlesex in the Inter Counties C.C. Championship. We won the Surrey C.C. title again and Len. Herbert won the individual prize. Frank Abberton and Bill Lucas were fifth and seventh and therefore also received their Surrey colours again. In the Junior race we were second. Our boys ran well although narrowly beaten by a fine South London H. team. Eddie Short was second, Arthur Bruce, third, Martin Williamson, fourth. Eddie Short was third in the London University Inter Collegiate C.C. Championship, held at Roehampton over five miles. He also finished third in the London Varsity Match against the Paris Varsities, held in Paris. We must welcome another Varsity man in Martin Williamson, who is at Cambridge. Martin has shown great promise already, his sixth in the Club 7 C.C. Championship was a fine effort, as was his winning of the Junior Shield at first attempt. He is with good company in Belgrave and we are pleased to have him. Vic. Blowfield has won both the Club C.C. Championships this season. He has also been tipped by the newspaper boys to win the National. Well, he can, with reasonable luck behind him. Albert Frost, getting fitter, was fourth in the Hertfordshire C.C. Championship. Eric Herbert ran an excellent race to finish third to Gosney and Barry in the Civil Service C.C. Championships. After having had operations on both legs last summer, Tom Carter is running well again. We wish him the best of luck this season. It must be noted here that Harry Shields won both the Handicap prize in the Club 10 C.C. Championship and the “ Statue ” prize at the social the same evening. Quite what this proves we are not very sure, excepting that Harry can both run fast and then stand very still when he wishes, in the right order! The Socials resumed at Belgrave Hall have been fairly successful but we do need the support of our younger members and their girl friends. Please do come along next season, you will enjoy it. The Hon. Social Secretary has arranged for a coach to take supporters to the Southern C.C. Championship at Aylesford on 28th February. Fare is 6s. 6d. Leaving from the “ Granada,” Clapham Junction at 12.30 p.m. Also three coaches are being laid on for the Brighton Relay on 10th April. Fare is 10s. Details to be announced later, but let the Hon. Social Secretary have names as soon as possible. Past President Harry Hare sends his best wishes to all his many Club friends, through Frank Webb who met him the other day. We had the following members representing their counties in the Inter County C.C. Championship Len. Herbert, Frank Abberton, Bill Lucas, Surrey. Vic. Blowfield and Tommy Clinton, Middlesex. Albert Frost, Hertfordshire. Vic. Blowfield finished eighth in the race. The rest have asked me not to mention their performances! I will not. We have, with the exception of the Enfield Race, won every Open ” Walk so far this year. Our chances of winning the three R.W.A. Championships are quite high, although Bert East's illness might put him out of the Junior and will, therefore, weaken our team considerably. items.sum: Introduction to the club's new panel of track coaches and a letter from George W. Clay, newly appointed Chief Honorary Coach, explaining his effort-based training schedules, sprint relay training and coaching etiquette.
items.s: THE BELGRAVE TRACK COACHING SCHEME Introduction to the club's new panel of track coaches and a letter from George W. Clay, newly appointed Chief Honorary Coach, explaining his effort-based training schedules, sprint relay training and coaching etiquette. As mentioned by the Hon. Running Secretary in this issue, a Panel of Coaches has been set up to generally improve and help all our atheltes running on the track this coming season. George W. Clay has been appointed Chief Honorary Coach and upon his appointment has addressed the following letter to the Hon. Editor. Dear Editor,—Having been unanimously elected by the Committee, to the post of Chief Honorary Coach to the Belgrave Harriers, I feel it encumbent upon me to write something for the Belgravian, a little magazine with a big purpose. I must say I hope to try my very best to fulfil a need which in my opinion, has always been with every Club. In my jorneying round, I have found many good athletes, both ancient and modern, possessing opinons at great variance. This has often resulted in the bewilderment of the young athlete. So my first object will be, and indeed, has been, to have a chat with our very patient Assistant Coaches, in an endeavour to enlist their co-operation and it is my pleasure to report at this stage, how willing they are and how unanimous are they in their views, of the necessity for a basic plan of training. Now during the last few weeks I have been working, devising schedules, for events in which I am convinced the Club's weaknesses lie, to wit, the sprints, the 440 yards and 880 yards. The pace of the training will be based on actual times for the distances done by the athletes. For instance, an athlete whose average time for 100 yards has been 10.6 seconds, if scheduled to run the distance at a three-quarter effort pace, he will do it in 11.4, at half effort pace, in 12.3 and so on. I cannot give you here my complete “ effort ” tables. Incidentally, I have had some recourse to Webster and Hays, but my tables have been modified. In a month from commencing training an athlete will have a time trial and if in the trial he does the distance in 10.8, then his future training will adjust itself and his three-quarter effort will then come down to 11.7 and his half effort to 12.5. So you can see the scheme I have set down will be a self adjusting one. The Assistant Coaches will keep a record of each individual, on a card, which he will keep in alphabetical order. The information will then be available for the Track Captain, who collaborates with the Running Secretary. I will personally take charge of the sprint relay training, as I have seen so many failures, with first class athletes in this event due entirely to differences of opinions on “ change-over ” methods and lack of ability to work out pace and distance. I shall be guided in the selection of “ Trainees ” for this event by my Assistants, and I know I shall be able to rely on their choice. Now may I advise all of you to study my remarks on “ starting ” in the last issue of the Belgravian, and may I take this opportunity of asking you all to get away from the old orthodox method of starting. Please turn up at the track promptly so not to interfere with the schedule of training, remembering all the good manners due by laws of etiquette, to your Coaches. May I ask that the Coaches be not interfered with during their efforts, it is grossly unfair and has the tendency to reduce the confidence placed in them by the Committee in the minds of the trainees. Good luck to 1948 track efforts. Sincerely Yours, GEO. W. CLAY, Hon. Chief Coach.. The Chief Hon. Coach can be contacted at 5, Windsor Avenue, New Malden, Surrey. George W. Clay George W. Clay appointed Chief Honorary Coach Geo. W. Clay GEO. W. CLAY Hon. Chief Coach; address 5, Windsor Avenue, New Malden, Surrey GEO. W. items.s: WALKING NOTES AND RESULTS Walking column catching up on results since the last issue: Harry Churcher's 10,000 metres trials and French record in Paris (with Freddie Blackmore's report), his Dublin and Inter Counties wins, the London to Brighton, Club handicaps, the open walks, the Horwood Cup, the Club 10 Miles Championship and Police match, and hopes for the R.W.A. Junior. Although our last issue appeared in November, owing to difficulties with printing its production was held up for some time and consequently a number of results for the latter end of the track season were not shown. As these included a number of Club successes which may by now have been lost to memory or passed unnoticed by some of our less active members, the results in this issue will carry on from where I left off, viz. the 50 kilometres Championship at Eastleigh. Continuing with the 10,000 metres trials which were held during the summer, on 21st July, Harry Churcher led the field at Motspur Park, to put up the very fine time of 46.22.4, with Jack Rutland second in 49.48. A few weeks later Harry further improved on this time when, again at Motspur Park, he returned the fast time of 46.10.6, half a minute in front of Jim Morris, S.A.C. In our own promotion at the Olympic distance, Harry was not on his best form and after a tussle with Jim Morris eventually finished second. The crowning light, however, of Harry's track performances was on his visit to Paris when he set up a new French record, his time of 45.31 being 23 seconds faster than the previous best. We reproduce here the report on the race by Freddie Blackmore, Chairman of the I.A.A.F. Commission on Walking:— Paris, 7th September. Johansson's time (45.36 returned a week before at Stockholm) was much in mind as Harry Churcher and Jim Morris prepared to take on the Frenchmen Maggi and Courron at 10,000—and thus it was a great thrill to watch Harry win very comfortably in 45.31. Always within himself, he could have reduced this by 10—15 seconds and it would have been faster but for a misunderstanding at the half hour stage. It had been arranged to fire a pistol and mark the distance covered by the leader at this point, but unfortunately, the steward ran beside Harry for about 50 yards and when he actually fired the pistol Harry concluded that he was being cautioned and no doubt hoped he wouldn't feel any worse. He broke stride, eased up and took a lap to settle down again. Up to this point he had gone round with a maximum variation of 2 seconds in his lap times. After he had recovered from the shock he resumed this consistency, 1.49; 1.49; 1.50; 1.49, and so on. Meanwhile a battle royal was proceeding between Maggi and Morris with the big excited crowd on its feet. It was Churcher—Hindmar over again, only more so. Jim kept the Frenchman from getting inside, but when he concluded the Frenchman had had enough Maggi proved him wrong, got in front and stayed there to set up a new French record in two minutes faster than his previous best. Finishing times were:— H. Churcher 45.31; Maggi 45.49; Morris 46.12; Courron 46.29. Previous record 45.54.8 by Huard. In a second visit to Dublin on 20th September, Harry had a double success, winning both the mile and 2 miles. Added to all these sterling performances he won the Club Championship in a new Championship time of 14.11.2 and the Inter Counties 7 miles Championship at White City on August Monday. In the veteran class Bert East appears to have been quite prominent. On 31st July, he finished third in a Veterans A.C. Handicap, and a month later in a similar race gained first place. The Track Season terminated with our usual Club Handicap Meeting which immediately followed the 10,000 metres reported above. Bert East, still showing improvement, made his way to the front, with Harry Rouse and Reg Elson filling the other places. In the London to Brighton race which marks the end of the summer season, we encoutered the same bad luck which had befallen us in the other distance races. Ten of our walkers went off at the strike of seven, and we certainly hoped for a place at least. Colin Sutton, however, failed to please the judges at 22 miles and was ruled out. Although our other men walked up to expectations we could get no better than fourth place. Jack Baker, our first man home, was the only one to get inside nine hours. Gordon Doubleday, who completed the course in 47 minutes less time than last year, won a handicap prize presented by Charlie Poulter. The race was well supported by Club members and friends and with the weather in our favour, a good time was had by all. And so we come to the beginning of yet another winter season. This opened on 4th October, with the usual Club Handicap. 28 of our walkers turned out and a match with the Police provided an added interest. Harry Churcher soon showed that he intended to produce the same speed on the road as he had been doing on the track and eventually won by over 1½ minutes from Young Mac. with Bert East third. With our walkers in the first seven positions we had an easy win over the Police. The Novices walk on 18th October only attracted three entries and Jimmy Coates who is now developing into a nice walker won his first Club prize. The opens started as usual with the Highgate promotion over the hilly course from Parliament Hill Fields. We were without the help of Harry Churcher who was taking a well-earned rest, but with our scoring four in the first 14 we took team honours with 38 points to Enfield's 49. George Bentley was second in the handicap and the B Team second in the Team Handicap. A fortnight later in the Enfield Open, the local lads took advantage of their knowledge of the course and narrowly won from us by 3 points. And so we come once more to our own club open. Then entry of 248 individuals and 31 teams is believed to be an all-time record for a road race. Of these, 206 walkers faced the starter. Harry Churcher, racing for the first time on the road since the Club opening walk, unfortunately met with disqualification. Our old friends Surrey W.C. were out in full strength, and although we managed to secure scratch team honours it was only by the very narrow margin of one point. In the handicap section our “ C ” team secured first place and Bert East tied for third in the individual handicap. Len Fletcher's return to the field of racing was very pleasing, his position being identical with that in last year's race. Bert Webb took the prize for the first Belgrave in the scratch race without other award. The race once again received the support of many club friends whose donations to the prize fund enabled us to maintain our high standard of prizes. To them, to the R.W.A. officials, to the many club members who assisted as stewards and records, and to the clubs and individuals who supported the event we offer our most sincere thanks for their part in making the race a success. Our next event, the Horwood Cup Race on 13th December attracted 17 juniors. All our possibles for the National Junior were competing. Bert East, walking faster than ever, headed the field, and in returning a time of 56.20 set up a new championship time. Bert Webb was an easy second and George Bentley, still improving, third. Alan Robins, walking above his usual standard, won the handicap. The Boxing Day meeting produced a dozen walkers and a fine display was given by Harry Churcher and Bob McMullen. Gordon Doubleday walked well to take first place in the handicap, followed by Oliver second and Jimmy Coates third, taking his first handicap prize. So we come to the end of 1947 and embark on yet another calendar year. This opened with the Cambridge Harriers promotion at Bexley, when we returned to our last year's road form and with our scoring four in the first six secured an easy win. Harry Churcher, walking in fine style, left the rest of the field to win by nearly two minutes. Joe Coleman's last-minute effort took him up to fourth position with Len Fletcher and Bob McMullen close on his heels. The superiority of our scratch team men was further emphasised by the fact that they were placed second in the handicap section.. In the M.P.A.A. Open at Imber Court a fortnight later our walkers once again cleared the board. An added interest to the race was provided by the fact that the starters included both Harry Churcher and Jim Morris. After the first stages, however, Harry went away from Morris and at the end of the first lap was nearly a minute in front. This lead he increased over the second lap to win comfortably by a minute and a half. This time we had our scoring four in the first seven, in fact we finished 11 men in the first 21, a remarkable achievement in a field of 160. Alan Robins walked well above his usual form to win the handicap, and although he had not been included in the handicap possibles, our “ B ” team won the team event with George Bentley third in the handicap. The Club 10 Miles Championship a week later was well supported. Twenty-eight of our members turned out and with the addition of 15 policemen constituted a very fine field, a match having been arranged in conjunction with the championship. The outstanding feature of the race was Bert East's walking. After holding on to Bob McMullen for a considerable distance, he eventually left him and although finishing 2½ minutes behind Harry Churcher, who incidentally lost a little ground by taking the wrong road on the last lap, finished a minute in front of Jack Rutland to gain second place. Although we finished the first five, it looked obvious from the Police packing in mid-field that the match would be closely contested. Eventually, scoring 16 a side, we won by the narrow margin of 251 points to 277. By the time this issue is published, the R.W.A. Junior Championship at Bradford will no doubt be over. On recent form we hope to do well and in fact, add one more success to our already good record. Finally, our good wishes go to our “ Olympic ” possibles who we hope will annexe at least one title. THREE MILES ROAD HANDICAP Held on October 4th, and a record field was seen out. Len Marchant proved himself very fit by winning in fine style, and a newcomer in L. Bush was second with Ted Stimpson third. We hope that Ted will soon get back to his pre-war form which gained him an International vest It was pleasing to see old-timers such as Arthur Penny, Cecil Mains, Bert Footer, and many others still turning out for this annual event, and if numbers are any sign of strength it would seem as if we are in for a good season over the country. items.s: FIVE MILES C.C. HANDICAP Report and full result (53 runners) of the club Five Miles cross-country handicap of 25 October: V. S. Blowfield fastest, J. McDonald handicap winner; the table prints E. H. Herbert's actual time as 20.32. Held on October 25th, and again a very large field turned out including our G.O.M. of the country, George Still. George is now turned 70 years of age yet each Saturday he can be seen running over the Common, and he usually takes along a school of junior runners with him. Coming to the scratch race, this was won by Vic Blowfield with Dick Towndrow second and Ted Stimpson third. To beat the half-hour over our course is quite good running, so it can be seen that Vic put in some really fast running, which should gain him many honours before the season is over. Ron Minahan, Eric Herbert, George Chantler, and Mike Heard also ran well, and an interesting entrant was Colin Sutton, the well-known walker. The handicap was won by J. McDonald with K. R. items.s: MATCH v. OXFORD UNIVERSITY Report and placings of Belgrave's cross-country match against Oxford University at Wimbledon on 1 November, won by Belgrave 28 points to 50. Held at Wimbledon on November 1st, and we were very pleased to welcome the University runners on their first visit to our headquarters. They had sent a mixed team of first and second string runners, but proved no match for our lads, who filled the first four places. The placings in our club five miles were repeated with Vic Blowfield once again leading the field home. Scoring six aside the team result was: Belgrave H. 28 points, Oxford University 50 points. Actual placings were: 1, Blowfield 29.14; 2, Towndrow 29.20; 3, E. items.s: SOUTH OF THAMES "JUNIOR" RACE Report of the South of Thames Junior cross-country race at Dartford on 8 November, where Belgrave A were second team to Dartford H. and all four Belgrave teams closed in. Held at Dartford on November 8th, and a record number of teams had been entered. As winners of the previous year we had to find a new scoring team, and were pleasantly surprised to find our lads running so well that they secured second place in the team race. Eddie Short was our first man home in fourth position, and was well supported by Mike Heard 12th, Ron Minahan 19th, and Eric Herbert 27th. Charlton. Our club seven miles championship was held over Wimbledon Common on December 13th, and another large field tourned out. Len Herbert, the holder, was defending his title, but in a fast run race he was beaten on the run-in by Vic Blowfield. Dick Towndrow gained his first club championship award in being third, with a past-holder in Arthur Penny fourth, and Tom Clinton fifth. The sealed handicap resulted in a win for S. Charlton, who showed much improved form, with B. Eglinton second and W. Spencer third. items.s: "SAVAGE" SHIELD JUNIOR RACE Report and result of the club junior cross-country race for the Savage Shield, won by Martin Williamson from Eddie Short; J. W. Cook is printed 6th with a faster time (32.25) than 5th. The holder of the title, Derrick Burfitt, was a non-runner as Derrick is not doing anything over the country this season in view of the coming Olympic Games, in which he is on the list of "possibles." A very close and interesting race was seen between Eddie Short, Martin Williamson and Arthur Bruce. Eddie led for most of the way but was beaten on the run-in by Williamson, who thus won a club title in his first season with the club. We wish him long and continued success in our colours and our junior strength gives us great hopes for the future success of the club over the country. Mike Heard was unlucky in being a sufferer from that bugbear of all cross-country runners known as "stitch," and also went off the course near the end of the race and so did not finish. items.s: "MACHER" SHIELD C.C. RACE Report and result of the club 10 miles cross-country championship for the Macher Shield on 24 January, won again by Vic Blowfield; sealed handicap won by Harry Shields. Held on January 24th, this race for the club 10 miles cross-country was started, in the absence of our President, by Albert Macher. A good field of 32 runners faced the starter, including the holder Vic Blowfield, while Len Herbert and Tom Carter, 1946 winner, and Arthur Penny, winner in 1934, 1936, 1938 and 1939, also turned out. The weather was far from ideal, which is not unusual for this race, and at the half-distance Tom Clinton was leading Vic Blowfield and Frank Abberton with Len Herbert and Bill Lucas running together. When they came in sight of the finish Vic Blowfield was out in front followed by Frank Abberton, who had run a fine race, and Len Herbert beat Tom Clinton on the run-in for third position. Although Lea Herbert is recognised as our best distance runner, he has yet to win this championship, and we hope he will carry on to lead our runners in the District and National races, although at the time of writing this appears doubtful. The sealed handicap was won by that "old war-horse" Harry Shields, who battled through to the end, with Eric Herbert, maintaining his recent improved form, taking second award, and Con Abberton beating his brother Frank for third prize. items.s: CLUB BOXING DAY MEETING Report of the club's Boxing Day track meeting at Tooting Bec: 100 yards handicap won by Alan Sexton, two miles by J. W. Kennedy and three miles walk by Gordon Doubleday. Our annual track meeting was held at Tooting Bec, and although it was a really glorious morning our members were evidently still recovering from the effects of the night before, judging by the limited number who turned up. We managed to make up three heats for the 100 yards handicap, which resulted as follows: Heat 1—1, G. R. Lowers (2 yards); 2, A. C. Allen (8 yards). Heat 2—1, A. D. Sexton (3 yards); 2, W. D. Brown (2½ yards). Heat 3—1, L. G. Christmas (5½ yards); 2, F. Simmons (11 yards). The final was a grand race between the three heat winners, and in a "blanket" finish Alan Sexton was adjudged the winner with Les Christmas second and George Lowers third. The field for the two miles run was more numerous, although both Len Herbert and Derrick Burfitt were non-starters. The eventual winner was J. W. Kennedy off 350 yards, who put in a storming finish to beat Alan Bishop (260) with Eric Bishop (350) third. The three miles walking handicap was won by Gordon Doubleday, who turns out over the country and yet still manages to put up good performances when he switches over to walking events. G. R. Lowers G. items.sum: Preview of the 1948 track season: a coaching panel under George Clay, club championships at Tooting Bec on 5 June, planned junior and inter-club fixtures, and entries to the Running Hon. Secretary E. A. Duffett.
items.s: REVIEW OF COMING TRACK SEASON Preview of the 1948 track season: a coaching panel under George Clay, club championships at Tooting Bec on 5 June, planned junior and inter-club fixtures, and entries to the Running Hon. Secretary E. A. Duffett. The thoughts of our club members will now be turning towards training for the track season, and they will be pleased to know that your committee have gone into the question of coaching, and have appointed a panel of coaches under the supervision of George Clay. George is well known to those of our members who train at Motspur Park and club members will also recall his son Fred, who was a very good sprinter and later took up the 440 yards. Fuller details will be given to members at a later date, but I can assure you that George is going into the question of training schedules very thoroughly and will be only too pleased to help any member who wishes to improve his performance by training to a definite schedule. This being Olympic Games year, we are all hoping to see some of our members in the English team, and in view of the date of the Games, we have put our club championships earlier in the season than is usual. They will be held at Tooting Bec Track on Saturday, June 5ith, and it is hoped that members will "book" this date and support the championships to their utmost. For members' guidance a provisional list of club fixtures can be seen at the end of the Gazette, although we hope to arrange further fixtures as the season approaches. We have arranged our usual Junior match with the Whitgift Middle School at Croydon, and have also accepted invitations to take part in Junior inter-club contests with the Polytechnic H. and Highgate H. The "Gordon-Stewart" Trophy contest, of which we are the holders, is being held at Drayton Green Track on Saturday, May 8th, and we have also arranged matches with the L.A.C., Cambridge H., Shaftesbury H., Highgate H., Mitcham A.C., and the Metropolitan Police A.C. The club have booked Tooting Bec Track for several dates, and we have had to take some Monday dates, in view of the number of clubs now using Tooting for meetings, but I trust this will not deter our members from turning up in better numbers than they did last season. With the Olympic Games being the highlight of the season, I think the usual club programme will rather be oversshadowed, but with all the "cracks" concentrating on that vital period from Friday, July 30th, to Saturday, August 7th, when all the athletic events are being held, this should give some of our less prominent members a chance of proving themselves. items.sum: Editorial notes apologising for the gap since the February issue and reporting the 61st Annual General Meeting, its honours awards and the new officers, captains and committee.
items.s: Editorial notes apologising for the gap since the February issue and reporting the 61st Annual General Meeting, its honours awards and the new officers, captains and committee. Owing to various circumstances outside our control it has not been possible to issue the Belgravian as regularly as had been anticipated. It will be noticed that this is the first issue since February and many items have had to be passed over and others dealt with briefly. It is hoped that we will be able to publish more frequently in the future. * * * The 61st Annual General Meeting held at Belgrave Hall on Saturday, October 9th, was perhaps the biggest ever, as nearly one hundred and fifty members were present. The Hon. Secretary's report, which had been printed and circulated, was taken as read and the Hon. Treasurer explained in some detail the Balance Sheet. Upon the recommendation of the Committee it was unanimously agreed to award Honours Badges to Alan Sexton and Jack Stirling Wakeley: Alan for his A.A.A. and Southern A.A.A. successes in the Junior 220 yards championships and Jack for his wonderful performance in the 24 hours' walk which he won by covering 122 miles 1,411 yards. These two are special awards needing the endorsement of the Meeting, and this was readily given. We must also congratulate Alf Taylor on having the honour of Life Member bestowed upon him. Alf has done a large amount of thankless "Back Room" work, principally on the Social side, and few will forget the manner of his handling of our junior cross country members three seasons back; so that the honour is well deserved. Upon the recommendation of the Committee and with the unanimous approval of the Meeting, Bill Webb was elected to the Presidential Chair for the ensuing twelve months. In thanking the meeting for the honour they were bestowing upon him, he said that increasing family ties, plus anno domini, had finally caused him to relinquish the office of Hon. Treasurer, which he had held since 1924. Syd King (and his wife) were elected to the vacant office. Several new appointments were made: E. T. Bateman taking over the Field Events; Frank Simmons the Junior Section; Micky Pyer, Junior Coach; and new blood was introduced amongst the captains by the election of Vern Blowfield, Ted Stimpson, Len Grimshaw and Len Fletcher. The elected Committee have been strengthened by newcomers in Bert Mitchell, Dick Towndrow, Len Grimshaw and Bill True. So that with the "old'uns" hanging on we may look forward to even better times than those we have already celebrated. Alan Sexton Alan Sexton awarded Honours Badge for A.A.A. and Southern A.A.A. items.sum: Notes on the Olympic Games: Jimmie Bellchambers and Harry Evans appointed walking judges, and the Games performances of Bill Lucas, Willie Nankeville, Harry Churcher and Etienne Gailly, with greetings from Gailly and news of Fred Rowell.
items.s: Olympic Games. Notes on the Olympic Games: Jimmie Bellchambers and Harry Evans appointed walking judges, and the Games performances of Bill Lucas, Willie Nankeville, Harry Churcher and Etienne Gailly, with greetings from Gailly and news of Fred Rowell. Our congratulations to Jimmie Bellchambers and Harry Evans upon their appointment as Walking Judges. To have such an honour bestowed upon them is a mark of appreciation of merit and ability from the "powers that be." In their time both Jimmie and Harry were distinguished competitors, both having won high honours on the track and road, and they are still enthusiastic workers, both in the Committee room and at our sports meetings. For many seasons now they have officiated at all the main Championship meetings, both summer and winter. Most of the original nominations of members for the Olympics, for one reason or another came "unstuck" at the final trials, but a new star arose in Bill Lucas to join company with Harry Churcher, Willie Nankeville and Rene Howell. Bill Lucas was selected for the 5,000 metres because of his 3rd in the A.A.A. 3 miles championship. Bill eventually finished 7th in his heat in about 15 mins. 29 secs. Willie Nankeville ran magnificently in the 1,500 metres. His second place in the heat, about 15 yards behind the winner, Erikson of Sweden, in 3 mins. 55.8 secs., was an excellent performance and showed that Willie could use his head as well as his feet. The day of the final turned out very wet and the general conditions were none too good for either competitor or spectator. The race itself was very fast and Willie running exceptionally, eventually finished 6th in 3 mins. 52.6 secs., just under three seconds behind the winner, a time which before 1932 would have won an Olympic title. What really happened to Harry Churcher in the 10,000 metres walk we shall probably never know. He, however, won his heat in 46 mins. 26.4 secs., two seconds inside Olympic record. In the final, a "caution" in the early part of the race worried Harry considerably and he perceptibly steadied himself and afterwards never seemed comfortable and appeared to have lost confidence, finishing 5th in 46 mins. 28 secs. Of Etienne Gailly, running for his country—Belgium—better known to some of us during the war as "Steve" and his very gallant effort in the Marathon will probably be talked of in the future almost as much as the memorable "Dorando" marathon. Etienne led practically all the way and was first to enter the Stadium but he had run himself to a standstill and was eventually third, his time being 2 hrs. 35 mins. 33 secs. Since returning to Belgium he competed in the Inter Allied Games held in Antwerp and finished second in the 5,000 metres and he came back again to England in September and was second in the Britannia Shield cross country race at Halton. Etienne sends greetings to the Club and wishes to thank his many Belgrave friends for their kind wishes and thoughts. We were pleased to renew acquaintance with Fred Rowell, another war-time member; this journey he was Manager of the Canadian Olympic Athletic Team. items.h: Seen at Wembley during the Olympic Games.
items.sum: Light-hearted round-up of Belgrave members seen officiating and helping at Wembley and the road events during the 1948 Olympic Games.
items.s: Seen at Wembley during the Olympic Games. Light-hearted round-up of Belgrave members seen officiating and helping at Wembley and the road events during the 1948 Olympic Games. Our Running Hon. Secretary as Marksman, ensuring that the World's fastest athletes didn't have their fingers ⅛in. in advance of the correct position at the starts. He must be an expert now on starting blocks; and was probably glad he wasn't called upon to handicap the fields on accustomed A.A.A. standard times at any rate! Bert Ellsey judging Field Events and standing up well to the strain of hours of competition. Our announcer's voice (Arthur Cook to you) floating over the air. Harry Evans and Jimmy Belchamber judging the walkers; Syd Roberts stewarding and producing mysterious jugs of refreshment for the monarchs of the Judges' stand and doing a grand job on the Road Walk. Harry Parker recording on Marathon and Road Walk and sitting tight at other times when it rained too hard, ably assisted by Jack Chapple! Our General Hon. Secretary taking things easy after discharging his responsibilities on the 50 Kilos Walk—except when seen sprinting around the track from Judges to Chief Judge during the Track Walk; Dick Savage, a busy man of Road Walk and Marathon days, in charge of a coach; Charlie Poulter, Syd King, Percy Wright and their battalions of assistants all doing great work on the Road Walk; George Chantler first and last pointsman on the Marathon, an arrangement which permitted a good view of all that happened in the Stadium. Not forgetting Joe Turner with an "Omega" in his hand and sitting astride a white bench. And last, but not least, our portly friend and adviser, Wally Jewell, assistant referee and chief judge, complete with pencil and scoring cards and visibly thinning under the strain of the "photo finishes"; and away at Herne Hill Track Dr. Woodard was acting as chief medico to the cyclists. Chief Insp. Jack Bidgood was "on the job" for both Road Walk and Marathon, supervising the courses throughout their length. Yes, Belgrave were well in evidence—on the track competing for the honour of Britain, in the crowd witnessing unforgetable sport and performances—and wherever wanted, giving a hand with the big and little jobs which go to make up the tremendous organisation of the World's largest sports meeting. The Senior, Junior and Youths championships were held at Aylesford on February 28th and it speaks well for the arrangements that these three races were carried through on the same afternoon. The hospitality extended by the local Paper Mills was on the highest scale and will long be remembered by the competitors and officials alike. In the Junior (under 21) event there were 20 teams and we did well to finish in 6th place. Eddie Short led our team home in 6th position, Mike Heard was 12th, Eric Bishop 27, and Len Bishop 68. Others to finish were: L. A. Adams 83, R. Garwood 88, and S. G. Brooks 106. The senior race was over a 10 miles course and from the start Sydney Wooderson went in front followed by Vic Blowfield, with Ted Stimpson also well up. Len Herbert was coming through well and Frank Abberton and Tom Clinton were also well placed. items.s: The English C.C. Championships. Report of the English (National) cross country championships at Graves Park, Sheffield, where Belgrave won the senior team title for their fourth National victory, with Vic Blowfield second to Sydney Wooderson. These were held in Graves Park, Sheffield, on March 13th, and being a fine day a very large crowd watched the racing. There were tremendous fields for all three races, Senior, Junior and Youths. Once again Sydney Wooderson was up the front but this time there was a small bunch of runners with him including our own Vic Blowfield. On the last lap Wooderson made his effort but Vic kept with him stride for stride and then about half-a-mile from the finish Vic made a gallant attempt to get away from his man and succeeded up to a point. The only snag was that there was further to go than Vic had thought and Wooderson came again to beat Vic up the finishing straight. Len Herbert had run well throughout as had Ted Stimpson, now getting back to his pre-war form, and with Frank Abberton also making a last lap effort, and Tom Carter and Tommy Clinton coming along well we found to our satisfaction that we had beaten Sutton Harriers, the holders, to record our fourth National victory. Les Stokell was once again a good 7th man and Albert Frost and Dick Tobin completed our team. Positions were: 2 V. S. Blowfield; 12 L. W. Herbert; 15 E. S. Stimpson; 27 F. J. Abberton; 41 C. T. Carter; 57 T. P. Clinton; 64 C. L. Stokell; 95 A. E. Frost; 132 R.W. Tobin. Team scores were: 1 Belgrave H., 154; 2 Sutton H., 174; 3 Blackheath H., 183. In the Junior race Eddie Short was again our first man home in 7th position, and to gain such a high place in a race speaks well for Eddie's strength and determination. Mike Heard also ran well in finishing 40th and Arthur Bruce ran pluckily on a damaged foot to be 56th, with Eric Bishop 65, R. Garwood 112, L. C. Bishop 117, and L. A. Adams 138. In the team race we were placed 8th out of an entry of 30 clubs so can be well satisfied. items.sum: Report of the London to Brighton road relay promoted by the News of the World, won by Belgrave in 3 hrs. 57 mins. 29 secs. after Bill Lucas overtook Max Jones on the last lap, with a stage-by-stage account.
items.s: The Brighton Relay. Report of the London to Brighton road relay promoted by the News of the World, won by Belgrave in 3 hrs. 57 mins. 29 secs. after Bill Lucas overtook Max Jones on the last lap, with a stage-by-stage account. The classic of the road relays, "the Brighton," promoted by the News of the World, was held on April 10th, starting from Mitcham Common. The weather was kind, there being bright sunshine without much heat, and a large party of supporters accompanied the team along the road. The finish of the race was most dramatic and those of us who saw Bill Lucas start off thirty-one seconds behind the Birchfielder on the last lap, thought it was all over bar shouting, and continued in a rather leisurely way into Brighton. Bill, however, had other views and maintained that lazy-looking but devastating stride of his right up to Max Jones who was leading. Max was unable to respond to Bill's challenge and there was a mighty roar from the crowd when it was realised what was happening and Bill eventually reached the finishing line just 20 seconds to the good. Truly a wonderful finish and reminiscent of that of years ago when Brickwood of Mitcham beat our own Arthur Allum in the finishing straight. The start of the race was far from impressive from our point of view, Ted Stimpson being unable to keep the fast pace set by the other runners and finished at Purley Corner 71 seconds in arrears. Tom Clinton ran a good leg and handed over to George Lucas at Merstham in sixth place. George started with supreme confidence on his 4½ miles jaunt up Redhill and along the switchback to the Prince Albert where he handed over in second place, clocking 22 mins. 36 secs., only 4 secs. slower running than Birchfield who were now leading. Over the next stretch of nearly five miles, Tom Carter took us to within two seconds of the leader. Ken Stimpson on the next stage to the Half Moon at Crawley, about 3½ miles—easily passed his opponent and handed over to Martin Williamson well in the lead. Martin ran extremely well to maintain this advantage to Handcross with a margin of 13 seconds in hand. The next leg to Hickstead, about six miles, is considered as perhaps the stiffest and most important, and Vernon Blowfield was up against Bobby Reid, "Sidney" and Stan Belton (Surrey). After a terrific struggle Vern. was barely a yard ahead of Reid at the change over, with Wooderson some distance in the rear. On to the foot of Dale Hill, about 4¾ miles, Len Herbert was never comfortable and eventually finished 35 secs. behind the Stagbearers. Eddie Short had Dale Hill to climb (shades of Bert Footer) but ran splendidly, in to Pycombe, although he was only able to reduce the Stagbearers lead by 4 secs., and so on to the Brighton front to see Bill Lucas turn the corner of the Aquarium ahead, to our frenzied delight. The time for the whole journey, 3 hrs. 57 mins. 29 secs., was the fourth fastest in the present series. items.s: Surrey County Road Relay. Report of the newly instituted Surrey County road relay at Woking, won by Belgrave, who became the first holders of the Underhill Trophy. This newly instituted championship was held at Woking on the 25th September and nine clubs entered teams of six men, each to run a lap of just under three miles. Willie Nankeville, our A.A.A. 1 mile champion, led off and gave us the lead from Surrey and Mitcham. Len Marchant kept the lead and then Stan Davies went off and running with a badly blistered foot he allowed the Surrey men to get within two seconds of him. Eddie Short went next and running a well judged race went right away to give us a 40 seconds lead. Archie Bedford was our next and he kept the lead so that Bill Lucas ran home an easy winner in 1 hr. 30 mins. 27 secs. Surrey A.C. were next in 1 hr. 32 mins. 5 secs. and Mitcham A.C. third in 1 hr. 34 mins. 24secs. We thus became the first holders of the "Underhill" Trophy awarded to the winning team, and our thanks go to the Old Woking Club for the splendid tea which they provided after the race. items.s: With our Road Men. Notes on Belgrave members in open road races during 1948, including wins by Tom Clinton and Dick Towndrow, the club Marathon championship won by Frank Abberton for the new A. F. Mitchell trophy, and A.A.A. standard medals. Quite a number of members have been competing in open road races this season and "Champ" Smith has done a good job in keeping them together. We were also pleased to see Bert Footer out again and showing that he is still a force to be reckoned with at distance running. Tom Clinton has also done very well and he won the Portsmouth A.C. 10 miles race on March 29th when we finished second in the team race with Tom Carter 7th and Dick Tobin 11th completing our team. George Chantler finished 6th but was running for our "B" team who were placed 4th while our "C" team finished 6th out of an entry of nine teams. On the 17th April in the Walton 10 miles race, Tom Clinton finished first with Tom Carter fifth, Geoff Pearson 14th and Bert Mitchell 16th. We won the team race beating Reading. Dick Towndrow won the 15 miles road race promoted by the Wigmore Harriers, and Geoff Pearson and Con Abberton finished equal fifth. In the Finchley "20" Geoff Pearson was 17th in 2 hrs. 13 mins. 31 secs., quite a creditable effort. On the 8th May our lads went to Chichester for the 16 miles road race to Portsmouth and Dick Tobin was our first runner in 8th place, Bert Footer 9th, Bert Smith 10, George Chantler 14, Con Abberton 15, J. McDonald 18, Tom Carter 24, and as we had entered two teams they actually tied for third place in the team race and Bert Footer won the toss for "B" team as to whom should take the prizes. In the Kent County open 20 miles event our lads ran well to beat the Polytechnic and Blackheath in the team race. Our positions were: G. R. Chantler 5, C. Abberton 6, A. Smith 8, G. M. Pearson 9, J. McDonald 10. In the Bexhill 16 miles road race on August 28th George Chantler was 12th in 1 hr. 42 mins. 35 secs. and Bert Mitchell 19th. This year we held our own Marathon championship, in conjunction with the Polytechnic race from Windsor to Chiswick, and after a good race Frank Abberton was the first to have his name inscribed on the new "A. F. Mitchell" trophy. The evergreen Bert Footer was second, only seven seconds behind, and George Chantler gained third place. The following gained A.A.A. standard medals:— F. J. items.sum: Review of the 1948 track season: Belgrave members at the Olympic Games, Alan Sexton's A.A.A. Junior 220 yards title, junior relay successes, the Youths section, and the retained Gordon Stewart Trophy.
items.s: The Track Season. Review of the 1948 track season: Belgrave members at the Olympic Games, Alan Sexton's A.A.A. Junior 220 yards title, junior relay successes, the Youths section, and the retained Gordon Stewart Trophy. On the whole I think we can be said to have had a fairly successful season and we had the satisfaction of seeing three of our club members compete in the Olympic Games as members of the Great Britain team. Actually another member, E. Gailly, was a member of the Belgium team and put up a magnificent performance in finishing third in the Marathon race. Will Nankeville also ran the "race of his life" by finishing 6th in the 1,500 metres final and when one looked through the list of those qualifying for the final, this was indeed a sterling performance. Harry Churcher and Bill Lucas also performed well without actually "hitting the high-spots" and cannot be said to have let the team down, rather was it a question of our men being outclassed by the wealth of opposition they were up against. We also competed in the "Kinnaird" Trophy and "Waddilove" events and also took part in an inter-club contest at the opening of the new sports stadium at Brighton. An encouraging feature was the promise shown by some of our Junior members and in Alan Sexton we have one of the finest young sprinters in the country. Alan crowned a successful season by winning the A.A.A. Junior 220 yards championship and another good performance at this meeting was Michael Paxton's win in the 440 yards. Our Junior sprint relay teams also did well in winning the Surrey County 4 x 110 yards and being placed second in the A.A.A Junior event against strong opposition. We are badly in need of a few first class sprinters for our senior matches as Lionel Grimshaw had muscle trouble and Gordon Lowers was not always available. Len Marchant and John Cope were our mainstays in the middle distance events and as usual we always had plenty of men to call on for the long distance races. Micky Pyer has been looking after our Youths section and has made a first-class "discovery" in M. J. Stearman. This lad looks a second Derrick Burfitt, having much the same style, and he won the Surrey County Youths 1 mile title in fine style. Also at this meeting D. E. Marshall won the 220 yards and being a school-mate of Alan Sexton's we expect still better performances in the future. Charlie Smart came home from Germany to compete in the A.A.A. meeting and ran well in both the six and the three miles without quite catching the selector's eye. George Lucas and Len Herbert had what was to them rather a disappointing season and we hope that a full season over the country will see them both fighting fit for next track season. Reg. Ruddick won the Surrey County 6 miles track title and should prove a great help to our teams when he is qualified to represent us. We once again won the "Gordon Stewart" Trophy put up by Ealing Harriers and had many enjoyable matches against both new and old friends. E. Gailly E. items.sum: The cross-country correspondent's look back at last season's successes and preview of the coming season's fixtures, from the Surrey Youths race to the English championships and Brighton Relay.
e: South of the Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: OVER THE COUNTRY. The cross-country correspondent's look back at last season's successes and preview of the coming season's fixtures, from the Surrey Youths race to the English championships and Brighton Relay. I said at the opening of last cross country season, that given a fair “rub of the green” we had the men who could sweep the board, so far as the “open” championships were concerned, and I must say that our lads more than justified our high hopes. To win practically all the major events of the cross country season and then carry on to win the “classic” London to Brighton Relay was, I think, a performance that will take a great deal of beating. With the help of Dick Towndrow, and such as Archie Bedford, Eddie Short, Mike Heard, “Ginger” Kennedy and Jack Brown, to mention only a few of our promising members plus the help of last season's stalwarts, I think we shall have yet another successful year over the country. December 4th sees the first of the County championships with the Surrey Youths race, and youngsters between the ages of 16 and 18 who wish to compete should turn up at Belgrave Hall and contact Micky Pyer who is in charge of the training of our juniors over the country. The following Saturday we have the first of our Club Championships and as there is a sealed handicap in conjunction here is an opportunity for all members, both fast and slow, to show their paces. On December 18th we have our 5 miles (under 21) race for the Savage Shield, and here again we are holding a handicap open to all members between the ages of 16 and 21. Boxing Day sees the usual track meeting at Tooting Common and there are events open to sprinters, runners, walkers and shot putters, so make a note of sending in your name and don't forget the meeting starts at 11 a.m., as last year a few turned up in the afternoon and so had a wasted journey. New Year's Day is County Championship day and we shall have teams in both the Surrey and Middlesex County events, as our members who are qualified to run in the latter race compete as members of the Cadogan A.C. and should contact Frank Webb if they wish to enter. On January 15th we have a visit from the Thames Valley Harriers for a social run. January 29th is the day of our club 10 miles race for the “Macher Shield” and we shall be pleased to see our old friend Albert Macher present the shield to the winner. We then come to the “open” championships and on February 12th the South of the Thames 7 miles race is due to be held at Horsham, followed a fortnight later by the Southern Counties events at Sandhurst. March 12th is the day of the English cross-country championships and the venue is the Bromford Bridge Racecourse at Birmingham. We can be sure that Birchfield Harriers will make a strong bid for the title on their own door-step, but hope that once again we can bring the title down South, and given the proper support I am sure we can do it. We then have the usual crop of open Road relays, culminating in the London to Brighton race, which if we win this year, will set up a new record for the total number of wins by any one club but will also be our second hat-trick of victories, a feat also performed by no other club. As usual we shall have our supporters coaches on the road and those wishing to book seats should make early application to the Social Hon. Secretary, Dave Shepherd. It will be noticed that we have “B” team matches and these are intended for those members who do not get a chance to represent the club in the big races. We hope to arrange more of these as the season progresses and members wishing to take part should keep in touch with the cross-country captain, Alf Taylor. Once again I wish all our members a very successful season and any further information as regards fixtures, training, etc., I shall be only too pleased to help in any way I can. E. A.
