items.label: November 1941
items.sum: Report and results of the return North of Thames v. South of Thames match at Parliament Hill Track on 30 July, won by the North 73 points to 50, levelling the series.
items.s: North v. South (Return). Report and results of the return North of Thames v. South of Thames match at Parliament Hill Track on 30 July, won by the North 73 points to 50, levelling the series. As the first fixture between teams selected from North of Thames had proved so successful, a return match was arranged and duly took place at Parliament Hill Track on the 30th July. The weather was not too good and the track on the heavy side, but a fair muster of athletes were present, although the North contingent rather outnumbered the South, who sadly missed M. H. Broadbent, the young Wallington schoolboy, in the sprints. In the 100 Yards, Bill Bowers ran extremely well, to be narrowly beaten by A. E. Chapman, the Middlesex County sprinter. W. Elliott again won the 880 Yards for the North, and is running very consistently this season. Len Marchant ran well, to finish second, and did excellently to split the North runners. S. Jarlett was a notable absentee from the 440 Yards, and we had to rely upon W. H. Watts, who ran a fine race, to only just be beaten by E. N. Day, who has had a very successful season. Quite a big field turned out in the 1 Mile, including M. Bingham, H. Pascoe, G. F. Morris and A. Hughes for the North, while the South had H. F. Saunders, G. Blackburn and H. W. Shields. The race resulted in a win for A. Hughes, not to be confused with A. (Lofty) Hughes of Reading A.C., but who promises to make just as big a name for himself in the athletic world as did his namesake. Saunders ran very well, to finish second with M. Forde, another Finchley Harrier taking third place. The 220 Yards saw Metcalfe, the tall Poly. boy, just beat Bill Bowers, who had to be content with yet another second place. A good field also turned out for the 2 Miles race, and here again the North runners were more numerous than for the South. Les Cohen continued his recent good running by beating Pascoe, the long-legged North London Harrier, in a ding-dong battle down the straight, with Attryde taking third place for the North. The final running event was the 1 Mile Medley Relay, and in this Len Marchant gained his revenge by just beating Elliott over the half-mile stage, but Metcalfe gained on Bowers, and Chapman went off in front of Simmonds, who had to give ground to a better man, so that Pettit had an 8 yards lead over Watts for the final quarter. Watts, however, pegged his man back in fine style and drew level with him in the home straight, and with ten yards to go, Pettit faltered and Watts nipped by him to win a very fine race. A 2 Miles Walk was again included in the programme, and a good field of walkers turned out, but the race was a virtual walk-over for E. A. Staker, the Highgate Harrier. The South were without Fisher, and actually the North filled the first three places. In the Field Events the South missed D. L. Grigg, the Met. Police athlete, but Quarton did well to gain second place in the Weight Put and third position in the Long Jump. Bill Sutton also did well in taking second place in the Discus and third in the Weight. The Javelin was won by the ever-green George Pownell, who is still showing the youngsters how to throw a javelin correctly. The South had the first two in the High Jump, and E. Solomon beat the promising Mitcham youngster, A. J. Ford, for first place. The scoring was on the basis of 5—3—2 and here the North had an advantage, as in some of the races the South had one representative only. All those who took part voted the match a success and as the North victory levelled matters, it was suggested that a " rubber " should take place at an early date. items.sum: Report of the final evening match of the season at Tooting on 13 August, in which the combined Belgrave-Polytechnic side beat the Metropolitan Police 51 points to 42. In the results (B) marks the Belgrave-Polytechnic side and (P) the Police.
items.s: Match v. Metropolitan Police A.C. Report of the final evening match of the season at Tooting on 13 August, in which the combined Belgrave-Polytechnic side beat the Metropolitan Police 51 points to 42. In the results (B) marks the Belgrave-Polytechnic side and (P) the Police. Our final evening meeting of the season was held at Tooting on August 13th, when the Metropolitan Police provided the opposition. As the Police Championships had been held the previous Saturday, there were several title holders present, but our lads rose to the occasion in fine style and won five out of the seven track events. In the 100 yards, M. H. Broadbent, the Wallington schoolboy, who has now joined the Club, won in fine style, with W. H. Bowers second and M. J. Wright third, but for scoring purposes the Police runner was given third place. The 880 Yards saw Len Marchant run his best race of the season to decisively beat the Police Champion, R. Ayton, who is also a member of the Mitcham A.C. In the 440 Yards another Police Champion came to grief when Syd Jarlett came through in fine style to beat W. R. Moody. W. H. Watts gained third position for us and has proved a fine second string to Jarlett in our 440 Yard races during the season. We were strongly represented in the 1 Mile as Doug. Wilson, the Poly. crack miler, was present, and A. Hughes, the Finchley boy, also turned out for us. Needless to say, the race proved a two man affair, and Hughes made Wilson go all the way in order to win. By winning the 220 yards, Broadbent completed a very fine double for one so young, and here again we had the first two home, with B. D. Metcalfe of the Poly. gaining second place for the combined Belgrave-Polytechnic side. In the 2 Miles, however, our distance runners received a rude shock when H. F. Saunders, the Police C.C. Champion, ran clean away from his field, which included Les Cohen, Tom Carter and Frank Abberton. Right from the crack of the gun, Saunders went to the front and, lap by lap, increased his lead over the opposition. His time of 9 min. 46.8 secs. is I think the fastest two miles time of the season down South, and considering the cold and windy conditions, it was a very fine performance indeed. The 1 Mile Relay was also a very close and exciting race, and over the half-mile stage Moody for the Police " jumped " Syd Jarlett with 300 yards to go, and gave his team a lead of 15 yards. M. J. Wright gained on Matthews over the first 220, and then Bowers all but caught Simmonds on the second 220, but a bad change-over resulted in Ayton going off about 5 yards in front of Len Marchant. The latter gradually caught his man, but Ayton had sufficient left to beat our man down the home straight and so score the second of the Police track wins. In the Field Events the Police fared better aided by D. L. Grigg, who had a very busy evening in winning the Weight and Discus and securing third place in the Javelin. Bill Sutton was second in the Weight and also gained third place in the Discus, but Bill seems to miss the support of Syd Jones, our other " strong " man, who is in the Services. Charlie Melchior once again obliged in the Javelin, and moreover is very consistent with his throwing. Our Field Events captain, Charlie Jones, showed an improvement in his long jumping by gaining second place in that event, being beaten by the Police Champion. Thus on the evening we scored 51 points to the 42 of the Metropolitan Police, and thank them for a very enjoyable match. items.sum: Report and results of the third North of Thames v. South of Thames meeting at the Enfield F.C. Stadium on 13 September, a Grand Display and Sports for the National Air Raid Distress Fund, won by the North 43 points to 40 to take the Lord Mayor of London's trophy (the text says 'North of London').
items.s: Match at Enfield Stadium. Report and results of the third North of Thames v. South of Thames meeting at the Enfield F.C. Stadium on 13 September, a Grand Display and Sports for the National Air Raid Distress Fund, won by the North 43 points to 40 to take the Lord Mayor of London's trophy (the text says 'North of London'). On Saturday, 13th September, the third meeting of the teams representing the North and South of Thames took place at the Enfield F.C. Stadium. The meeting had been billed as " Grand Display and Sports," and was in aid of the National Air Raid Distress Fund, sponsored by the Lord Mayor of London, who was present at the meeting. The Lord Mayor had very graciously presented a trophy to be held by the winning team for twelve months, and so a contest which only came into being this season will now be carried on for many seasons to come and will, we hope, take its place beside such meetings as the " Kinnaird," etc. As the Belgrave and Shaftesbury Clubs were responsible for the idea, they have agreed that this competition shall be confined to clubs in membership to the North and South of Thames Cross Country Associations. To return to the actual meeting, the South team was very much handicapped by the fact that on the same day there was a meeting at Surbiton to which the Met. Police had promised support, and so the South of Thames team were denied the help of any of the Police athletes. Also quite a number of our lads were unable to turn out, and as these included Broadbent, Dumbrill, Jarlett, Watts, Carter, Smart, also Bryan, of Eastleigh, the South team was very much weakened. Actually for the seven running events we had only seven athletes, six being Belgrave and one Mitcham. In view of this, the performance they put up was little short of marvellous, and all seven of them are to be heartily congratulated on their fine sporting spirit in carrying through the contest and on providing such a close and exciting match. The 100 Yards was won by J. Wigley, the T.V.H. sprinter, with A. E. Chapman second and W. H. Bowers third. Wigley repeated his win in the 220, but this time Bowers moved up a place, with Metcalfe of the Poly. taking second place. For the 1 Mile we were especially pleased to welcome none other than Len Herbert, our Club Champion, who was home on leave, and he showed that he had lost none of his old form by winning in the very creditable time of 4 min. 35.2 secs. Les Cohen gained second place for the South, with H. Pascoe taking third place for the North. In the 3 Miles the South were represented by Frank Abberton and Harry Shields, who has now taken over the track captain's job, as Frank Webb has been called up to the Forces. Frank Abberton caused quite a surprise by beating his field and seems to have regained his old form and should have a good season over the country. S. G. Worboys of Woodford Green was second, with the local runner L. G. Bettiss taking third place. This brought us to the 1 Mile Medley Relay, and the South team was:— Herbert, Bowers, Hayes, Marchant, which made the third time of running for Marchant and Bowers, and the second for the other two, which speaks volumes for their pluck and sportsmanship. What is more, they won this event, beating the North team composed of Pettit, Metcalfe, Chapman and Day. Also in the programme were a 2 Miles Walk—and here again we have to thank the R.W.A. secretary for his very kind co-operation—and one field event: the Weight Put. It was impossible to include more field events as there were no jumping pits on the ground, and the other displays prevented a Javelin or Discus event being held. We were very glad to welcome Syd Jones in the Weight, and he won with a fine put of 38ft. 11in. Bill Sutton took second place, with D. McLaren of the North third. The 2 Miles Walk was won by E. A. Staker in fast time, and D. Christie-Murray, the Surrey W.C. and Oxford University athlete, finished second, with A. W. Marler of the local club third. Taking the scoring as in the previous contest, i.e., 5—3—2, with the Relay 3—0, the points worked out:— North of London 43; South of Thames 40. Thus the North take the trophy for the present season, but we hope to continue these very sporting and pleasant fixtures when next season comes along—old Nasty permitting—and wish to thank all concerned for making the contests so entertaining and enjoyable. items.label: November 1941
items.sum: Review of the club's 1941 track season, covering the A.A.A. open handicap meetings, the Southern Junior Championships at Chiswick and thanks to the officials at club meetings.
items.s: Review of the 1941 Track Season. Review of the club's 1941 track season, covering the A.A.A. open handicap meetings, the Southern Junior Championships at Chiswick and thanks to the officials at club meetings. We have every reason to be satisfied with this season's results. We have had some very keen, close, and enjoyable matches, and I am sure all our boys have enjoyed their racing. The winning or losing of these matches does not matter, and so long as our chaps can enjoy some competition, then our aim in arranging these matches has been achieved. The A.A.A. Open Handicap meetings have been well supported, and I trust they will be continued next season. At the Tooting Bec. meeting on June 7th our Field Event captain, Charlie Jones, won the Long Jump Handicap, and G. Hayes, who has been assisting us this season, won the open 220 Yards. The meeting at Charlton Park on July 5th saw Tommy Morrell gain third place in the 1 Mile Handicap, and A. Readman was second in the 2 Miles Walk. It was at this meeting that our " infant prodigy," M. H. Broadbent, showed his paces when winning the Open 220 Yards off 15 yards. At the Southern Junior Championships held at Chiswick on June 21st, Broadbent had been narrowly beaten for the 220 yards title, while A. H. Lomas ran very well in the 1 Mile, but could not get placed. Also at this meeting was an Open 2 Miles Team Race, and in this our lads, Les Cohen, Charlie Smart and Tom Carter, tied for first team prizes with the Shaftesbury boys. As our chaps had secured premier team honours the previous season, they decided to let Shaftesbury have that honour this time, a gesture which was much appreciated. The Marathon Race for the " Sporting Life " Trophy was also decided at this meeting, and was won by G. A. Humphreys, an Ilford lad running in the Woodford Green colours. Tom Richards, the Mitcham Welshman, was second, but all the runners appeared affected by the heat, and C. H. Ballard, of Surrey A.C. must be accounted unlucky as, when leading by a good margin, he collapsed near the ground and was unable to complete the course. In the many representative matches held during the season, the name of Belgrave appeared many times, and all those honoured are to be commended upon keeping the name of the club to the fore. In particular we would like to thank those gentlemen who so kindly officiated at our club meetings—Joe Turner and Charlie Hill, who came along as timekeepers—A. G. Fell, our very efficient starter—Charlie Cook, our " lad " with the tape—and also Charlie Jones and Dick Savage, who undertook the managing of the field events and, moreover, made a very good job of it. We look forward to the 1942 season and trust that we shall once again have all the lads back with us again, and until then wish them God speed and the very best of luck. items.label: November 1941
items.sum: Report by the Field Events captain on the 1941 field events season, naming the club's mainstays, guest helpers and outstanding performances.
items.s: Field Events. Report by the Field Events captain on the 1941 field events season, naming the club's mainstays, guest helpers and outstanding performances. The past season, in spite of a further reduction in active members, has been very successful. Ron Jeal, Charlie Melchoir, George Powell, Bill Sutton, a promising new member, L. J. Higgins, together with the Field Events Captain, have been the mainstay. We decided, in common with other clubs, to invite members of other clubs who would otherwise be short of competition, to assist us in carrying out our season's programme, and we have to thank A. W. Lewis (Epsom), J. S. Rugman (Shaftesbury) and A. J. Ford (Mitcham) for their help. Both Syd Jones and Laurie Jackson also helped us when on leave. Outstanding performances of the season were Syd Jones's shot putt of 38ft. 11in. and Bill Sutton's 36ft. 1in. in the same match at Enfield; Ford's high jump of 5ft. 8in. at Tooting on the eve of his joining the Forces; Melchoir's javelin throw at Imber Court against the Police. Rugman was very consistent with his long jumping, doing over 21 feet every time out. In the season's open handicaps Higgins won the discus and was second in the shot at Charlton, and Charlie Jones won the long jump at Tooting. I wish to thank all the Field Events members for their assistance during the past season. T. C. Jones T. C. items.label: November 1941
items.sum: Walking notes reviewing a busy wartime summer season, the new winter programme and the club's walkers called up or serving on the R.W.A. Southern Committee.
items.s: Walking Notes. Walking notes reviewing a busy wartime summer season, the new winter programme and the club's walkers called up or serving on the R.W.A. Southern Committee. Despite the fact that a large proportion of walkers are now with the Services, we are able to look back on the summer season, just finished, as one of the most active on record. The R.W.A. Southern Committee, and its very able secretary Mr. McSweeney, are to be congratulated on their endeavours to keep walking on the top line and their fine lead in promoting open walks has undoubtedly encouraged the promotion of further events which have taken place. It is definitely pleasing in these difficult times, and a sure sign that walking is on the up grade, to have included in the summer programme two entirely new ventures, the London Transport 5 Miles Open, and a series of track handicaps organised by the Metropolitan W.C. In past years, a number of walkers have lain off during the summer, for a well-earned rest after the long winter walks, but this year has seen no break at all, and entries in all events have maintained an extremely high level. Walking events were also included in the four A.A.A. Meetings, and also three Charity Meetings, held in aid of various War Relief Funds. The winter season, just commenced, was given a good start, again by the R.W.A., with a 5 Miles Open from our own Headquarters at Wimbledon. A good programme has been arranged and will be added to as time goes on. Our own " Open " will take place, as last year, in March. Black-out conditions prevent us from holding it at the usual time, but we hope to be able to revert to November before long. Bill Snell and Arthur Beales, one of our youngest members, are among the latest to be called up for duty with the Services. However, with the support of our Police members, and the efforts of Service men to conveniently arrange leave to coincide with walking fixtures, we are still able to field a team strong enough to do the club credit. Congratulations are accorded to our popular club member, Jack Bedgood, who very ably stepped into the breach as Chairman of the R.W.A. Southern Committee following the call-up of Alf Harley. With his subsequent re-election as Chairman for the present season. and the inclusion of Syd Roberts on the Committee, we are assured that our interests in that quarter are in safe hands. Once again, hearty greetings to all our walkers in the Services, with a renewed hope for a safe and speedy return. Mr. McSweeney Mr. McSweeney secretary of the R.W.A. items.label: November 1941
items.sum: Walking notes by the Chairman of the R.W.A. Southern Committee, signed J. C. Bidgood, on wartime race walking, Alf Harley's wedding and news of walkers in the Services.
items.s: WALKING NOTES. Walking notes by the Chairman of the R.W.A. Southern Committee, signed J. C. Bidgood, on wartime race walking, Alf Harley's wedding and news of walkers in the Services. Race walking in the South is still going strong in spite of the war and the calls which it is making on everyone. In the R.W.A. Southern Committee's Annual Report for 1940-41, the Secretary recorded that the second war year was one of remarkable activity. That will not be disputed, and what is even more pleasing is the promise of even greater activity in the season which has just begun, as a glance at the fixture list will show. Fields are smaller than in normal times, as of course they must be, but the spirit is still the same, and we may be sure that when peace comes there will be enough willing hands ready to help bring the sport back to where it once stood—and beyond. The last issue of " Belgravian " recorded Alf Harley's engagement. Since then he has " been and gone and done it," and we must now congratulate him again. For my part, I must not say too much on the question, because it was my good fortune to serve as his best man—(Yes, she was a very nice bridesmaid!)—but I think it is important to record what I am sure we all feel, namely, that Mrs. Alfred Harley will, when peace and normal times return, spare him for Belgrave's cause on Saturday afternoons at least, even if those glorious Sunday hikes may not see him regularly as of yore. Percy Wright's News-Letter still arrives regularly and with unflagging verve. The idea was a brilliant one, and Percy deserves our greatest thanks. How the devil he gets the information so promptly and accurately down in the wilds of Wales I do not know! Walkers will be pleased to know that Bill Snell, now in Ack Ack Beer Beer down Aberystwyth way, is well and cheery. He aired his walking shoes and a Belgrave Club vest within two days of becoming a soldier, which can't be far short of a world's record! Frank Elson came up to see us and the R.W.A. Open 5 Miles Handicap at Belgrave Hall on October 4th, but we couldn't persuade him to turn out. He'd been eating Purser's Pudding or splicing the mainbrace, or something like that, but promised to see about it next time. J. C. Bidgood J. C. items.label: November 1941
items.sum: A life member's recollections of Belgrave Harriers between 1902 and 1914: headquarters, training runs, races on the Embankment, the trainer and the club's early supporters.
items.s: NOTES ON THE BELGRAVE HARRIERS. A life member's recollections of Belgrave Harriers between 1902 and 1914: headquarters, training runs, races on the Embankment, the trainer and the club's early supporters. I think the present members of the Belgrave Harriers will be interested to read some of the past incidents in connection with the Club, from the years 1902—1914, as I remember them. Your President, F. G. Thompson, is, no doubt, more qualified to quote prior to 1902. Frank Bool being the Hon. Secretary, and Sam Sherrington the Captain. The headquarters were removed from the " Kings Arms " to the " William IV." on the Embankment; our training runs being from Grosvenor Road to Albert Bridge or round Battersea Park railings, over the Albert and Chelsea Bridges, 3½ miles approximately. Later, we had cross-country quarters at the " Railway Tavern," near Wandsworth Common, our course being across the Common, over the " Cat's Back "—our name for the small bridge over the railway—across some fields (long since built upon), Mitcham Lane and back—7 miles, races (excepting cross-country) being held on the Embankment, Pimlico. These were mostly held in darkness, only gas lighting—a miserable yellow glow, no incandescent mantles those days—the light from an oil lamp (cycle) at the fiinishing post aided the writing of names of placed men. Incidentally, the lamp usually blew out. The judges claimed each placed man on these occasions and did not "let go" until he had established his identity. I have known races held so late that it was difficult for those who required a " pick-me-up " to get dressed to get down to the bar in time (and the closing time then was midnight). After a race or training spin you arrived back to a nice hot bath, prepared by our trainer, Bill Harland—that is, if you were first home; after that it got thicker and thicker, probably the forerunner of the " mud pack." The trainer then got busy with the flesh gloves. Once up and down on the front, taking the legs in his stride, two on the back, and a smack on the rump, finished you at 2d. each. We made our own oils and used them. We all had different ideas, and the smell of whisky, turps, vinegar and what not, made the place reek. The principal entrant in our Boxing Day sprint was A. N. Other, to be handicapped, he was in most heats, late entries, and some who said they had posted them on? But you generally got less start than you expected in that case. Some remarkable finishes were seen, one I remember was as near as possible a "dead heat" between four. Someone placed them, but I couldn't. B. C. Donlevey was the handicapper. Did he know your form . . . ? the closest handicapper ever. . . . About this time our captain, Sam Sherrington, won the Haig & Haig Challenge Cup for the third time, and it became his own property. This was replaced in later years by the H. T. Blackstaff Shield. The first big advert. for the club was when H. A. Smith finished third in the Brighton Walk. About this time our members were getting among the " open prizes." Membership grew steadily. Amongst the supporters, without whom I think the " Bells " would have faded out, were W. J. Pepper, B. C. Donlevey, D. Chatterway, A. P. Fletcher, R. W. Ricketts, J. Thompson, J. Wilcox, T. Nicholson, H. A. Smith. This, of course, was at the most critical period. I find that I have covered a considerable amount of space. Not yet, however, have I told of the boxing section. The birth of the walking section, the various inter-club events and " skits " on some of my dear old pals, anecdotes of the past. The worst paper chase ever, the team medals we won and lost. items.label: May 1942
items.sum: Letter from a member at an R.A.F. officers' mess at Halton thanking club friends for a wedding present received at Belgrave Hall.
items.s: Letter from a member at an R.A.F. officers' mess at Halton thanking club friends for a wedding present received at Belgrave Hall. Officers' Mess, Halton, Bucks. March 23rd, 1942. Dear Harry,— I should be most grateful if you would extend the very sincere thanks of my wife and myself to all those good friends who wished us well on the occasion of our marriage, and subscribed towards the very handsome present we received last Saturday when at Belgrave Hall. It will be a constant reminder of happy times spent among good friends; and we hope the time is not far distant when it will be possible to enjoy once again the joys of sterling friendships and good sport in peaceful surroundings. With renewed thanks and good wishes. Sincerely Yours, ALF. Halton Belgrave Hall

items.sum: Reminiscences by a serving member appealing for Forces members to write for the Gazette, recalling past club personalities, walks, cross-country triumphs and track men, and naming promising younger members.
e: South of the Thames Senior Race
items.s: MAINLY REMINISCENT. Reminiscences by a serving member appealing for Forces members to write for the Gazette, recalling past club personalities, walks, cross-country triumphs and track men, and naming promising younger members. Each month sees a wider distribution of our members over the Earth's surface—each month lengthens the distances between us—each month makes the " Belgravian " more and more of a necessity. Our Gazette is a reminder of happy times spent together in sporting endeavour; and a reminder that the prized friendships we have built against a background of amateur sport and happy associations, still exist; and will continue to exist even when the War is recalled as something rather unpleasant which came our way in the distant past. The great majority of Club members are now serving in the Forces and look forward to the arrival of the " Belgravian " giving news of friends and of the athletic events which continue to be held. As one of this great majority, may I suggest that those away from the Club should make their literary contributions to the columns of the " Belgravian"? Don't leave it all to the minority who bravely carry on; let the hundreds of members in the Services express themselves in what is our Club journal, and with this in view, send your piece along to Harry Parker. Considerations of censorship must be borne in mind, but news of you and what you are thinking about Club matters and mutual friends will be of interest, and merit publication. Some of us find ourselves in unexpected places these days, and our memories work overtime. We re-live the incidents of past years, we wonder how this one is faring and where the other lays his head in these days of War. What does the Royal Marines think of Bert Footer, and is there an " issue " of " syrup of figs?" What's the news of our first cross-country International, Arthur Allum? Does Tommy Scrimshaw ever see a pair of spikes these R.A.F. days? Len Rollins is in the Navy, we hear, and we should be glad of news of our one-time enthusiastic Social Hon. Secretary, Cross-country Vice-Captain and helper in dozen of ways. We hope to see him a Club Vice-President in years to come. How does Fred Bentley find life in the R.A.F.? What does Harry Shields think of war-time rationing? And what becomes of Doub's meat ration? Is Frank Webb still the same old " Snaky "? How much walking does Tommy Green do as a Lieutenant in the Home Guard? Are Jimmy Flatt's legs still twinkling over the country? Is our President's health now improved? We all sincerely hope so. Who will promote a Veteran's Race for Charlie Cook to win in his eightieth year? How is our former President and Hon. Secretary, Wally Bayliss, these days? And Jock McKay, Harry Hare, Oscar Horwood and Teddy Gordon, to name four other Past Presidents? Is Ernie Duffett now the complete " cop "? Do Bill Sutton and Syd Jones still find time to toss the 16 lbs. shot about? Stopped any golf-balls lately, Oscar? How is our good friend Bill Fish these days? When does Jimmy Belchamber plan the next all-night Brighton stroll? Does Harry Parker use as many postcards as formerly, with postage 2d. a time? What's the latest Lindsey crack? When shall we shake Ken O'Kell by the hand again? Is Percy Wright taking out Welsh naturalisation papers? How's finances, Bill? . . . and so on, into the night. . . . We grow very reminiscent and memories succeed one another in rapid succession. We think of the disgraceful incident on Colley Hill when Harry Shields put the damper on Footer; and of a somewhat similar incident when Micky Walker saved a fiery situation on the way to Littlehampton; and of hundreds of other memorable things. There are thoughts of holidays with Club mates in Denmark, France, Germany, Switzerland, Devon, Isle of Wight; of Eastertide on the South Downs and in the Cotswolds; of Whitsuns in the Chilterns and on Derbyshire peaks. And I think of the Southern Cross-Country Championship at Brighton in 1930, when we were placed in this event for the first time, led by smiling Syd. Warboys in 13th position. And of the Club's team win in the South of the Thames Senior Race at Gatton Park the previous year, when the cheery President of the Association, our own Harry Hare, presented the " Dewar " Shield and " Colman " Cup to the Club—both for the first time. We think of the Brighton Relay of 1927, when we were placed seventeenth; and of those later years when Belgrave justified the hopes of the South. Our first " Southern " win at Taplow in 1934 comes to mind; and then, in 1935—" Belgrave Harriers—English Cross-Country Champions." How the writer remembers feverishly counting up the scoring discs—and his feelings of pride and excitement to find we were winners with a 54-points margin over Salford H.! Memories of Brighton Walks with Tommy Green, Fred Rickards and Fred Bentley to the fore, followed by many other stalwarts; of National 20-Miles Championships with George Cooper, Bob McMullen (Senior), Stanley Manning. Jack Rathbone. Joe King, Jack Bidgood and others, striving their utmost. Of Harold King and Len Fletcher, and in more recent years, Harry Churcher winning the shorter distance road walks; supported by as fine a bunch of sportsmen as ever stepped into racing kit. Of Charlie Churcher now miles away; of Colin Sutton, recently awarded his " Wings," of Frank Elson, Don Brown. the Colemans, Rutland. Charlie Speechley, and so on. The list is unending! We think of the superb Club track men such as Tommy Scrimshaw, Jim Tosh, George Dunckley, Eddie Pack, Cooper-Clark, Len Herbert; together with Bert Footer, Arthur Penny, Jim Ginty, Tom Carter, Les Cohen, Pat Parker, the Flowers, Jack and Joe, Arthur Allum. Ted Stimpson, and the others who have represented the Club with such distinction. The trouble with reminiscences is that they follow no set plan. The mind jumps the years, switches back again; dwells on the minor things to the exclusion of the more important. The small things stick in the memory, and the names and memories of the many who could never be champions. and yet were good friends and good sportsmen, remain. The pattern that is Belgrave is inextricably woven of good friends, good sportsmanship, happy memories, successful athletic endeavour, good fellowship, efficient democratic management, cheerful comradeship, grand workers, and a marvellous spirit. These things will continue; and the success the Club has enjoyed will carry on, for the same spirit permeates the younger members. We have walkers like Tony Bellchambers, Ted Elliott, Bob McMullen (Junior), W. H. Jones, and runners such as Bill Bowers, young Broadbent (who many of us would like to meet and wish well in his athletic career with the Club), Len Marchant, de Beau. Norman Shrubb, Edwin Read, and many others who will emulate the deeds of those who have gone before. Guided by the older hands and supported by all who have experienced the delights of Club membership in years past; Belgrave is assured of a wonderful future which will probably overshadow the glorious past, rich though it is in a hundred different ways. Good luck to all who have the good fortune to wear Belgrave colours, past, present, and future! A. A. HARLEY. items.label: May 1942
items.sum: Letter from a member in Norfolk recalling training-night memories at headquarters and wishing all members a safe return.
items.s: Letter from a member in Norfolk recalling training-night memories at headquarters and wishing all members a safe return. Tritton, Nr. Gt. Yarmouth, Norfolk. February 2nd, 1942. Dear Officials and Members,— Since hearing from your loyal Secretary I feel it encumbent upon me to drop a line to you all. Although like a good many other members far from the field of present and past activity, I still daily, deeply and very often think of past events. Especially the smell of winter green and the whisper in one's ear: " Have you a bit of vaseline to spare?" etc. Not always a Scottish whisper either. Then I must'nt forget the gentleman who turned up for training with no shorts but was so keen that ultimately, after searching the hall with no success, accompanied me in his trucks with the ever useful safety-pin. I often wonder how our dear judges are. The people you often thought had a double because they moved about so quickly. Are they in the Army, watching the troops march? My health has greatly improved recently, and I know it will improve more if I could see the great line up in Lauriston Road as in pre-war days. In conclusion, I wish every member a safe return to the Club Colours as soon as possible. Not forgetting our President, Mr. F. Thomson, whose health, I sincerely hope, has greatly improved. Cheerio lads; best of luck and health to everyone in the future. Yours sincerely, H. THAXTER. H. Thaxter H. THAXTER F. Thomson Mr. F. Thomson President Tritton Gt. Yarmouth Lauriston Road

items.label: May 1942
items.sum: Run of club notes: a Flight Lieutenant promotion and a suggestion for reunion Saturdays, thanks for the club Christmas card, members serving abroad, thanks for the Supporters' Club, the walking Open, help flagging the course, and keeping in touch with members in the Forces.
items.s: Run of club notes: a Flight Lieutenant promotion and a suggestion for reunion Saturdays, thanks for the club Christmas card, members serving abroad, thanks for the Supporters' Club, the walking Open, help flagging the course, and keeping in touch with members in the Forces. Congratulations to our Alf on gaining another " Ring." His title now is Flight Lieutenant. He sends many interesting letters and makes many happy suggestions for the benefit of the Club. One of his latest and best—in my opinion—is the following:— " To fix up Saturdays during the year when ALL members, and ALL OLD TIMERS would be expected to make a very special effort to turn up." Once upon a time the Opening Run of the Winter Season, which took place the first Saturday in October, was always looked upon as a " Reunion." A group photo was taken and many old friendships renewed at such meetings. But in later years, the " Opening Run " seems to have dropped out of fashion. I can see no reason, however, why it should not be revived. Another " Reunion " day could be the first track meeting. Can we have your support? * * * * Did you get your Christmas Card? For this effort our best thanks are due to Joe Coleman, who carried out the working drawing and made the printing block, and to Alf. Harley for the general suggestion and design. The idea you can follow? To others I would mention that we have at present, members in many parts of the world, including Australia, Canada, U.S.A., Finland, Norway, France, Iran, with the Forces in the Middle East and elsewhere, and all over the British Isles and Ireland. * * * * The thanks of ALL members are due to Les Cohen, and his Wife, for their unfailing zeal and efforts in making the Belgrave Harriers Supporters' Club such a stupendous success during this last season. They have both done a wonderful job of work, and believe me, the Hon Treasurer is truly grateful. What! Never heard of the B.H.S.C.? Well, just ask Les about it when you next see him. * * * * Thanks are due to our energetic Walking Secretary, Syd Roberts, for his efforts in the Club Annual " Open." The Hon. Treasurer is more than gratified with the result, as Syd made the race pay for itself. * * * * The Hon. Secretary wishes to put on record his appreciation for the help given him by Dick Savage and Bill Webb on Saturday afternoons, during this last Winter Season, in ALL weathers, in flagging the course. Also to Fred Puleston, of Mitcham, for his help in the same cause. * * * * It is the desire of the Committee to keep in touch with all members who have joined H.M. Forces. Will any who have not yet done so, kindly advise the Hon. Secretary? If you have forgotten his address, write to Belgrave Hall. items.label: May 1942
items.h: LETTERS AND NEWS HAVE BEEN RECEIVED FROM:—
items.sum: Members' news column with short notes on Belgrave members serving in the Forces and elsewhere, from letters received.
items.s: LETTERS AND NEWS HAVE BEEN RECEIVED FROM:— Members' news column with short notes on Belgrave members serving in the Forces and elsewhere, from letters received. Bert Smith (" Smiffy ").—A staunch Belgravian and team man of a few years ago, and who has now joined the N.F.S. L. Jackson (Field Events), who writes from " Sunny Devon ": " Must say how grateful I am to have received my copy of ' Belgravian.' It certainly brings back many happy memories. Hoping you will excuse quick letter, as I'm just on my way out for a pint!" W. H. Applebee, H.M.S. " Proserpine," finds opportunity to send along his subscription and to wish the Club the very best of luck for the future, and hopes it will not be long before he can again help to swell the chorus, " Up the Bels," on the Brighton Road. Jack Shields, in the R.A.F. in Buckinghamshire, says " There is very little opportunity for running here." Bill Snell.—On his way overseas, and who has taken his Belgrave togs with him. A. C. Beales is now in Ottawa, Canada. Colin Sutton has now " graduated " in Alberta, Canada, and contacted another Belgravian—Reg. Shepherd. Rodaway, D. A.—In Wiltshire. Training as a pilot in the Fleet Air Arm. Has already gained his Wings. Bill Merryman, now a Corporal in Staffs. Has got his O.C. interested in running and brought a team to Mitcham for Joe Bink's last relay. Stan Blunden, now in Hampshire doing his P.T. with Sergt. Dumbrill. Freddy White.—News has reached us that Freddy is now married and a Corporal. Stationed somewhere in the Thames Valley, he won six firsts for his R.A.F. Station during the last track seasons. Arthur Beaumont.—Now taking a P.T.I. Course at Bulford. Also enjoying a spot of football. Tommy Green.—Now a Lieutenant in the Home Guard. Teddy Gordon.—A R.S.M. in the Home Guard. Don Brown.—Playing Rugby in Lincolnshire. Megaphone Man " Cook."—Not liking Redcaps has transferred to the R.A.S.C., and is now in Dorset. Colin Sutton, from whom a very long and interesting letter has been received from Medicine Hat, has gained his Wings and hopes to be home again very shortly. Tried distance running at Calgory, but found the rarified atmosphere too much, but is still doing a little walking and running. Mrs. Shepherd writes to say that her son Reg. is in Saskatchewan, with the R.A.F., and will forward him the Gazette. Reg. will be remembered as a very promising junior of a couple of seasons back. News has just been received that Reg. has now " graduated." Tommy Clinton, our Guardsman, is now happily married. Congratulations Tommy. Ron. Patience has now returned from the Shetlands, is also married. Dick Towndrow.—Still in Northern Ireland, but has been on the sick list and missed the Irish Senior C.C. Race. He competed in the International Race at Belfast, and finished about 41st. He, however, won two big Open C.C. races before Christmas. Jack Rutland has been in hospital with pneumonia; is now on the convalescent list, but missed his Overseas Draft. Bob Stride, whilst waiting to go overseas won his Brigade C.C. Race and 4th in the Divisional Race. Charlie Churcher.—A very interesting letter sent on his way out East, describing 48 hours' leave in Cairo and a visit to the Pyramids—a dance—finishing up with supper of eggs, chop, chips and tea. Dinner on Sunday was eggs, liver and chops—chicken—beans—chips, roll and butter, tea and then ice-cream. And he cannot see the faces of the women because they are veiled! Join the R.A.F. and see the world free of charge! Had a Camp Sports Day, and won a half-mile walk in 3 m. 40. Frank Jeffries, in the R.A.M.C., and now in Cornwall. " Champ " Smith is now a " full blown " cook at Tidworth. Stimmo has again been home on leave from the Orkneys. Watts, E. J.—A Corporal in the R.A.F., and down Southampton way. Ken O'Kell.—Still in the North helping in the production of 1260-h.p. aero engines. Quackenbos (" Quack ") sends his best wishes to the Club and all members from the U.S.A. Although thousands of miles further away from Belgrave Hall than most members, he still finds time to write home. Last summer won 2 Statuettes and 10 medals, chiefly in longer track races. Norman Shrubb, home on short leave, brought back Press photos of the International C.C. Race in Belfast, on March 21st. He has recently become engaged to the sister of Teddy Read, our well known sprinter. Teddy, until rececntly, was with the R.A.F. in Canada, but has now returned home with his " Wings." C. T. Pateman, R.A.F., Slough, sends his best wishes to all members. Jimmy Kemp, from Northern Ireland, where he says Army boots and plenty of work keep him out of running togs. Was very impressed by Dick Towndrows' win in the M'Connell Cup Race. Michael (R. G.), R.N.—After a course of instruction on a dry land ship on the South Coast, has since gained a Commission. Congrats Mike. Ben May, also on the South Coast training " Faireys." Joe Coleman, who is seeing England at the expense of the R.A.F.. Had so many addresses lately that he doesn't know where he is! Frank Webb.—Keeps us well informed with news from Northern Ireland. Has finished 15th and 16th respectively in two big Open C.C. Team races. Was 32nd in the Irish Senior C.C. Race, which he says was one of the worst courses he has ever run over. Finished 90th in the International Race at Dublin in a field of about 350. At the Irish C.C. Race he met another member, Lieut. A. J. Marsden, of the Ox. and Bucks., of whom more news is awaited. He congratulates the team on their recent successes. Alf. Orton.—Now a Corporal in the R.A.F., Middle East, where he arrived after a monotonous two months' voyage. Douglas Mumford, we understand, has now gained his " Wings." Bill Sutton spent Christmas Day at Catterick, and says he " did not do too bad." Sid Jones, our weight slinger, has gone out East, and more news is awaited. Charlie Redgrave, having passed his Dental Exams. at Chatham, has now been sent to Skegness. Herbert Clayton, with the R.A.F. in Aden. Sergt. G. F. Long, Royal Marine Division, writes: " Thanks for ' Belgravian.' Greatly appreciated." Frank King, who has been " stationed at a very exciting spot . . . consisting of 3 cottages and a bunch of heather," has now been transferred to the R.A.S.C. Robert Boyden writes from Wiltshire:—" Thanks for ' Belgravian,' it was much appreciated. I notice I am in the list of " lost contacts." I got married January last year, on the 13th for luck." Congratulations, Bob. Bill Bowers writes from Scotland, where he is undergoing a course of instruction in wireless training. Tom Scrimshaw, in a " hush hush " district in the Midlands, writes: " What really spurred me on to this noble effort was that I received the Mag. All sorts of very pleasant memories flashed through my brain. I missed Ken O'Kell by a split second in a Midland town the other day. Pity you didn't write before Tom, as Ken would be very pleased to renew acquaintance. He also says Len Rollins is in the Navy. And also wishes to know if E. A. Good has ever seen a handicap made by Ernie Duffett! Les. Bennett.—The last news was received from Singapore. We sincerely hope he is safe. Jack Flower.—Belated news that he is in Iraq and is sporting " one Pip and a Sam Browne." From Exeter.—News has just reached us that Doubleday (" Doub ") is safe and returning to London as soon as possible. Sergt. Pilot Bill Lucas, " Somewhere " in Cambridge, Nov. 25th.:— " Pleased to have news of the Club. Remember me to all the boys, and I shall be glad to hear from any of them. I usually manage to get out for a run once a week." Commenting on his " Ops," he says:— " I have 12 trips to my credit. It gives us much pleasure to see our bombs burst on their targets and to know that we have done a little to help the war effort. My feelings on my first trip—actually it wasn't half as bad as I had expected it to be. I think our shakiest ' do ' was returning from . . . . after a successful attack. . . . The wind changed . . . . and we drifted over Kiel. The ground defences allowed us to get nicely placed . . . how they missed us I still don't know. . . In the next few minutes we had a most hectic time." Extract from a letter from a walker down Hampshire way:— " Percy seems to be doing things the (w)right way, alright "! items.label: May 1942
items.sum: Walking notes on the road walking season, praising R. McMullen's improvement, reporting the club open walk and a wedding presentation to Alf. Harley, and sending greetings to walkers in the Forces.
items.s: WALKING NOTES. Walking notes on the road walking season, praising R. McMullen's improvement, reporting the club open walk and a wedding presentation to Alf. Harley, and sending greetings to walkers in the Forces. WALKING NOTES. Since our last issue, another Road Walking season has almost passed by, and although the Club Colours have not been quite so prominent amongst the leaders as in pre-war days, those who have been left to carry on have spared no effort to ensure that when these troublesome times are over, our Club mates on active service will be able to pick up the threads where they left off and once more carry the maroon and amber to victory. Our most improved walker this season is, without a doubt, R. McMullen. Starting off at the beginning of the season, well down the field, Mac has gradually worked his way up, improving each time out, his best performance being in our own open, when he was third in the Scratch Race and winner of the Individual Handicap. Coupled with this were a tie with his club mate, F. Halls, in the Surrey W.C. promotion from our headquarters on 27th December, 2nd place in a club handicap on 29th November. and first in the club handicap on 7th February. Such rapid and consistent improvement augers well for the future, as Mac is still only a youngster and also a " Junior." Our Club " Open " this year proved a great success, the entry being the second largest of the season, and 15 more than last year. Unfortunately, owing to an error in declaring the teams, Mac got in with the wrong lot, and we were thus deprived of winning the Scratch Team Race. However, we had first and a tie for third in the handicap, and also third handicap team. Percy Wright walked splendidly to finish 4th in the scratch race and tie for third in the handicap. Alf. Harley, who was accompanied by Mrs. Harley, acted as Referee and Starter, and at the conclusion of the race, before calling on Mrs. Harley to present the prizes, Jack Bidgood handed them a silver teaset, as a token of congratulations from the Club on the occasion of their marriage. A number of welcome visitors included Harry Churcher, Len Coleman and Frank Elson. Percy Wright is still despatching his News Letter regularly. As it is only possible to send out a limited number, members are earnestly requested to pass it on as quickly as possible after having digested its contents. Jack Bidgood has been appointed a member of the A.A.A. Southern Sub-Committee for Walking. A full summer programme has again been arranged, and it is hoped that these events will receive the support they deserve. Once again we send hearty greetings to our walkers in the Forces, at home and abroad, with a sincere wish for a safe and speedy return. R. McMullen R. McMullen most improved walker of the season; 3rd in Scratch Race and winner of Individual Handicap in the club open; tie with F. Halls in Surrey W.C. promotion 27th December; 2nd club handicap 29th November; 1st club handicap 7th February; a Junior R. McMullen R. Mc-Mullen F. Halls F. Halls tied with R. items.s: SOUTHERN COUNTIES C.C.A. Reports and Belgrave placings for the five Southern Counties C.C.A. cross country races of the 1941-42 winter, four of them won by Bingham of Finchley and one by Bryan, with Belgrave winning the team race each time. SOUTHERN COUNTIES C.C.A. Five Cross Country races were organised by this Association. The first at Belgrave Hall on October 18th received an entry of 14 teams, comprising nearly 100 runners. Bingham, of Finchley, led from the start and eventually won in 30.59. Dan Patience ran very well to finish 3rd. It was pleasing to see Arthur Penny, Alf. Taylor and Bert. Mitchell out again, although obviously short of training. Syd. Ring travelled up from Oxford, but Len. Herbert, coming down from Staffordshire, arrived too late to start. Dick Towndrow, home on leave from Ireland, finished 5th. 3, D. Sixteen teams entered, and about 120 runners faced the starter. The start was a very fast one and soon had the field strung out, and once again Bingham was in the lead. Although chased all the way by Carter and Patience, he again was first home in 28.40. 2, Carter (28.49) ; 3, D. The third race was held on December 13th, at Ruislip, under the auspices of Finchley Harriers, over a 5-miles' course. Although 14 teams had entered, not more than about 80 runners faced the starter. Our fast men have not yet got the measure of Bingham, who over his own course ran home comfortably to win in 32.32, despite a great effort on the part of Les. The fourth race, which was to have been held at Cranbrook, was transferred to Caversham under the direction of Reading A.C., and was held on February 21st. The course was 5 miles over hilly country, which gave the spectators splendid views of the race. Owing to the inaccessability of the venue and a bitterly cold day, only a few keen supporters were present. The race was a " carve up " from the commencement between Bingham, Bryan and Carter ; all three hanging on, and it was very obvious in the second lap that Bryan, who was forcing the pace, had the measure of the other two. items.label: May 1942
items.sum: Report of the News of the World relay at Mitcham on 6 December 1941, won by Belgrave's reserve team after Marchant's fast leg and Tom Morrell's last lap.
items.s: NEWS OF WORLD RELAY. Report of the News of the World relay at Mitcham on 6 December 1941, won by Belgrave's reserve team after Marchant's fast leg and Tom Morrell's last lap. NEWS OF WORLD RELAY. Postponed from November 22nd, owing to lack of entries, and held at Mitcham on December 6th. This date clashed with the Southern Counties' fixture with the Army and other Units at Hayes, and incidentally robbed us of the services of our team who were selected for the race at Hayes. In consequence the race looked a certainty for our rivals " Mitcham," more especially as their representatives selected to run at Hayes decided to support their Club. However " there's many a slip twix cup and lip." Mitcham won the first leg, with Tobin taking 3rd place. The next lap went to Epsom, with Bert Mitchell 3rd. Lindsay took the next lap and went up one. We were in for a surprise in the next lap. When the runners came in sight climbing the slope up the railway bridge, it was seen that Marchant was out on his own ; down the other side and round the pond Len was running grand, and his long and easy stride brought him home 1 m. 33 secs. in front of the second man—clocking 14.30 for his leg, a time only beaten by two internationals, Close and Fox. Speaight went away on the next leg full of running, and taking a " bashing " raced home all out, but still in the lead and clocking 15.42. Tom Morrell went off for the last lap with a do or die look on his face, and to the cheers of our supporters. Excitement was now very high, Mitcham, with Fox, being only 1.30 behind. But Tom made every mile post a winning post and, putting every ounce into his effort, ran home a winner, clocking 15.33. Tom was all out but he got there ! Congratulations. It was very pleasing to see Dick Tobin again, back from Ireland. Also Corporal Dumbrill, who was in the R.E.'s team from Hampshire. Also Frank Jeffries, who was with the R.A.M.C. team, from Hampshire. It was a pity that only four of the " B'. team turned up. As it was they went up from 17th to 12th place before packing up. items.sum: Report of the cross country match against the Canadian Army at Belgrave Hall on 14 February 1942, won by the Club 91 points to 209.
items.s: CANADIANS. Report of the cross country match against the Canadian Army at Belgrave Hall on 14 February 1942, won by the Club 91 points to 209. CANADIANS. On February 14th, 1942, more Club history was made. In the past we have entertained at Belgrave Hall many champions and many champion teams, including teams from Paris and Cambridge University. The war gave us the opportunity of inviting the Canadian Army in England to meet us in a C.C. match. A very representative team was sent, accompanied by many officers, including Lt.-Col. R. R. La Blatt, and a large party of supporters. The runners appeared very enthusiastic, but their star man, Elliott, was unable to compete, having just recovered from an attack of influenza. The usual 5-miles' course was used, and twelve aside to score. The day was fine with a sharp wind and a bright sun. Lt.-Col. R. R. La Blatt started the field of 35, and which included 17 Canadians. items.sum: Report of the Southern Counties 7 miles Inter-Counties race from Belgrave Hall on 10 January 1942, won by Tom Carter, with the result of the club handicap held with it.
items.s: INTER-COUNTIES RACE. Report of the Southern Counties 7 miles Inter-Counties race from Belgrave Hall on 10 January 1942, won by Tom Carter, with the result of the club handicap held with it. INTER-COUNTIES RACE. The Southern Counties C.C. Association promoted a 7-Miles Inter Counties race on January 10th, from Belgrave Hall, over our usual 7-miles course. The course was one of two laps, and first time round the leading bunch included Carter, Dan Patience, Draper and Bryan. With about a mile to go Tom Carter was leading Dan by about 30 yards, with Draper about the same distance behind, and Bryan fourth. This order was maintained to the finish, and Tom Carter showed that he was back to his previous season's running when he won 13 races right off the reel. Dan Patience, who had won the Middlesex title a week before, also ran well to finish second, and Army life seems to suit him well. R. H. Bryan ran his usual plucky and determined race to finish fourth, and by so doing he gained first place in the Club handicap which was held in conjunction. It had been originally decided to hold the handicap over a 5-miles course on December 20th, but owing to weather conditions it had to be postponed, so it was decided to hold it in conjunction with this race, and 18 Belgrave and 4 Polytechnic members supported the event. Second place in the handicap was taken by A. W. G. Peck, of the " Poly," who is running very well this season, and he actually beat Les Cohen in the scratch race. Third place went to Dan Patience, who beat that " little-un" Bert Footer by one second ! You should have heard what Bert said ! ! ! Len Marchant was unlucky enough to have another runner's spike through his heel in the first lap of the race and so had to retire. RESULT. Postn. Name Club Act. Time Start Hcp. e: North v. South of Thames track contest
items.s: NORTH v. SOUTH, 1942. Ernie Duffett announces the 1942 series of North v. South of Thames track matches and urges members, including those in the Services, to support them. NORTH v. SOUTH, 1942. Last season our members will remember that we held a series of contests on the Track between sides representing the North of Thames clubs and the South of Thames clubs. These contests first came into being owing to a Club fixture falling through at the last moment, and as the first fixture proved so successful it was decided to hold others, finally culminating in a fixture at the Enfield Stadium at which the Lord Mayor of London was present ; and he also gave a Cup to be awarded to the winning team, which was secured by the North after a very close contest. This season we are again holding a series of matches, two being at Tooting Bec., and two at Parliament Hill Fields. There will be running events from 100 Yards up to 2 Miles, also several Field Events, and the R.W.A. are also co-operating by putting on a 2-Miles Walk at each meeting. What I want to impress on all our members, including those in the Services, that they must look upon these meetings as Club fixtures as indeed they are, and all those who can come along on these dates will be more than welcome and can be sure of turning out for some active competition. It is practically impossible these days to arrange the old-time Inter-Club matches, and so it was thought that a contest on these lines would ensure a full programme of events being carried out and would also give a chance to those athletes belonging to less fortunate clubs than our own, to turn out and get a spot of some real competition. I understand that the Middlesex County are supporting the North in their endeavours to turn out a tip-top team, and although we cannot claim any such support, I am sure we would welcome the assistance of any athlete who belongs to a South of Thames club and who would like to come along and lend the South team a hand, or should it be feet? Our Track Captain is Harry Shields, who is still plugging away with the best of 'em, and his address is : 37, Hudson Road, Bexley Heath, Kent, and I am sure he would be very pleased to hear from any of our Service members who may be able to get to Tooting Track for a Saturday afternoon meeting. So don't forget, do your best to come along to all these meetings, whether home or away, and we will see if this time we can capture the Cup from the North ; and in any case no matter what the results so long as all those competing enjoy their afternoon's sport, then those promoting and officiating at these contests will think their efforts well rewarded. ERNIE DUFFETT. Ernie Duffett ERNIE DUFFETT Harry Shields Harry Shields Track Captain; 37, Hudson Road, Bexley Heath, Kent North v. South of Thames track contest Enfield Stadium Tooting Bec. items.sum: Appreciation of Harry Evans, the walker newly elected club President, recalling his racing career from 1908 and his long service as a judge and club member; it says he was back with the club "early in 1929" after the 1914-18 War, as printed.
items.s: HARRY EVANS. Appreciation of Harry Evans, the walker newly elected club President, recalling his racing career from 1908 and his long service as a judge and club member; it says he was back with the club "early in 1929" after the 1914-18 War, as printed. This year the Belgrave Harriers have honoured by election to the Presidential Chair the first of their members who attained a place among the fastest walkers of his day, and in return, he has honoured us by his acceptance of the position. Until the year 1908 we had had no walker of outstanding ability, but on Good Friday of that year Harry, after working on hot cross buns for 37 hours in the bakehouse, won an open two-miles handicap at Stamford Bridge, and followed it up by being placed in every two-miles handicap he contested until 1911. In those days Amateur athletics was not the clean sport that the watchful A.A.A. have now made it. Even at Stamford Bridge there was always a spot where an athlete could get a friend to put a little on either himself or a fancied rival. Entry forms, too, were different in those days, and the practice of working up a mark was easier and very prevalent. Harry would not countenance such a practice, and that he would have nothing to do with it is amply proved by the consistency with which his all-out efforts got him among the prize-winners. Cleanness and fairness was to him the essence of sportsmanship, and this is his outstanding characteristic in a life-long connection with athletics. Early in 1909 the Road Walking Association, then but recently founded, inaugurated a ten-miles Junior inter-team race. This blossomed, two years later, into the now well-known Junior Championship. Harry won this first race, and his time for the ten miles, 82 minutes 37 seconds, shows what a really fine walker he was. The course was a climb from the Thames Valley at Brentford over Hanger Hill, dropping to the Brent Valley, and back over the ridge again. In those days when motoring was in its infancy it was usual that about two miles of a ten-miles race would be on roads with a narrow strip of Tar-Macadam on its crown, while the rest of the journey would be over a much rougher surface. In making a comparison of the times then recorded and those of recent years allowance must certainly be made for this difference. In the years 1909 to 1911, Harry gained six first-class standards in the A.A.A. Championships, three at two miles and three at seven. He likewise put up many fine performances on the road, particularly at seven miles. As the champions during these years were G. E. Larner, E. J. Webb and H. V. Ross, Harry was certainly a star at a time when the stars were exceptionally bright. In the years 1912-14 his work prevented him from any serious racing, and just as he was ready to recommence, the War broke out. Harry joined the Forces and was soon in France. Early in 1929 he was back with the club however, and although he did not again reach his old form, he was a stalwart and useful performer for the club in team races at seven to ten miles. At these distances the club was now very strong. Bob Rickitts, the writer, Harry, Charlie Wells, Alec. Spendlove, Wil Hawker and Harry Hanger were a strong level seven, and during the next two winter seasons the club won almost every open team race at both distances. Harry was frequently in the scoring four and always well enough placed to add to the scores of our opponents. This successful team was not so strong as the more recent combination of the Churcher and Coleman brothers, Percy Wright, Colin Sutton, etc., but it brought the Club wery much to the fore. Up till now our attention had been given to shorter races, but for several years the writer had been drumming it into the others that, to make history as a road-walking club, we would have to turn to longer distance racing. At about this time (1920-1921) he succeeded, and in a few years we had good team for the twenty-miles Championship and the Brighton race. Harry, however, was a few years older than the others, and could not find the necessary time to train for longer distances. In 1921 he was elected to the list of Road Walking Association judges, and during twenty-one years he has enjoyed a reputation for sound judgement and fairness which is universally granted him by all,—Officials and Competitors alike. Frequently, too, he has judged at the A.A.A. championships. Many are the walkers, both in the Club and in the larger walking world who have profited by his judgment and advice. Indeed, it can be said with truth that all whom he has disqualified respect and admire him; so from all sides his election as President will be welcomed with the keenest pleasure. For many years he served the club, first as Captain and later on the Committee. For the past ten years or so, however, night-work has prevented him from attending Committee meetings; otherwise he woud certainly have held the Presidency of the Club before this. His tenure of the Office is in troubled times, but with the Club all is well; and he can rest assured that he will have the hearty support of all who are carrying its affairs on during the absence of the brother-members of whom we are so proud. items.s: CONGRATULATIONS. Congratulations from a member away on war service to Harry Evans on becoming President, and to the committee, Les Cohen, Michael Broadbent and Willie Nankeville. to Harry Evans and all good wishes on being electetd President. I know I voice the feelings of many unable to be present at the A.G.M. when I write that many who were far away at the time, wish they could have been present to support the feeling of the meeting, and add their vote to the unanimity which honoured one of the hardest working members we have ever had. Harry was winning Championships in the Club name before many of those of the present day were born; and throughout the years he has been a valuable helper and one of the keenest of Club members For years the nature of his job made it impossible for Harry to help our Committtee or to take those honours which were rightfully his; but war time restrictions on night work in his trade gives us the opportunity to honour him as we should have liked to do years ago. Harry has always worked hard for the Club in many unassuming ways. His Bozing Day Cake " swindles " will be remembered by many, his help to our social side has been tremendous, and his assistance as an official over many years has endeared him to all. Harry has the well-earned reputation of being one of the finest walking judges in the country (many would say " the finest "); and he has officiated at many A.A.A. Championships, and hundreds of other walks on track and road. Harry Evans is a man of strong character and has a deep attachment for the Club of which he has been a member for so many years; and in knowing him, we honour ourselves. He is a very worthy addition to a worthy list of Presidents. Congratulatins also to our Committee who have kept the Club alive athletically; and in difficult days arranged fixtures and entered teams which have acquitted themselves well in the accustomed Belgrave tradition. Congratulations too, to Les Cohen on his magnificent effort for the Club funds in difficult times. The Balance Sheet makes marvellous reading; and we are greatly indebted to Les and Mrs. Cohen for all their work on our behalf. Renewed congratulations to Michael Broadbent on his magnificent dual Junior Championship wins, which are the pointers of greater things to come; and to Willie Nankeville upon his Junior Championship success in the 880 yards. Congratulatins to all who have done something towards keeping the Club-spirit, that we know so well, alive; and ready to welcome us on our return from these far places to which war has compelled us.—We are grateful. items.label: October 1942
items.sum: Short letter from the new President, H. Evans, thanking members for electing him.
items.s: FROM THE PRESIDENT. Short letter from the new President, H. Evans, thanking members for electing him. To all Belgrave Harriers,— I thank you for the great honour you have done me by electing me your President. I never thought when I joined your Club in 1907 that I should ever become the President. It has geen a great pleasure to me to see the progress that our Club has made of late years. I only hope that we shall all continue that progress in the future, and keep up the Belgrave spirit. H. EVANS. H. Evans H. EVANS new club President; joined the club in 1907

items.label: October 1942
items.sum: Report of the war-time A.G.M.: tribute to retiring President Frank Thompson, the Hon. Secretary's review of the season, thanks to helpers, and election of Vice-Presidents, a Life Member, committee and captains.
items.s: THE ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING. Report of the war-time A.G.M.: tribute to retiring President Frank Thompson, the Hon. Secretary's review of the season, thanks to helpers, and election of Vice-Presidents, a Life Member, committee and captains. Another war-time A.G.M. has come and gone—and perhaps a more important one than the last, as the meeting decided to change its President. To most of us it has been a matter of great regret that Frank Thompson, owing to continued ill health, has been unable to take his rightful place amongst us. Frank, a 100 per cent. Belgravian, must have felt it most acutely. One of the earliest of members, never a great runner, but an enthusiast, he could tell you Club history from the foundation. He was a life member, had held most offices at various times; acted as Hon. Secretary a few years ago during a rather difficult period; became a Vice-President and lastly President. For some years he has been an elected member of the Southern Committee A.A.A., and had been through the Chair of the Road Walking Association. In latter years he had attached himself, during the winter season, to the walking side of the Club, and was well known throughout England as a top grade scoring judge. During the summer months, when walking was more for the individual (apart from teams), Field events were his pet and he could always be found with the " strong men " on the track at Battersea Park on a Sunday morning, always willing to give of his experience. He has been a wonderfully fine worker for the Club, and for both the A.A.A. and R.W.A.—he was keen and thorough and worked well on all the branches of athletics with which he was connected. All members will sincerely wish him a speedy recovery and a return to " Belgravian " life.—Frank—for what you have done, we thank you. * * * * In his report, the Hon. Secretary stated that the Club had again had a most successful season, despite the difficult and very trying times. During the last winter season the runners had won all five cross country team events promoted by the Southern Counties' Association, and had followed this up by winning all the open team races on the track in which they had competed. The walkers, on the other hand, had not been so successful as a team, but individually members had had a very fair share of the prizes in open events. The annual open walk had again been successfully presented, both athletically and financially, by Syd. Roberts. Some new blood was being introduced, and it was hoped that very soon the team would once again be on the top line. The summer track programme was necessarily very restricted and had almost resolved itself into North v. South of Thames competitions, under the very able guidance of Ernie Duffett. However, two junior fixtures have been carried out with success, and had unearthed much new talent, particularly in the way of high jumpers—sadly lacking in the past. Now we have several jumpers all around 5ft., and with the continued care of Charlie Jones it is hoped that 6 ft. will be reached by at least one, by next season. Three Southern Junior Championships had been won during the season, Michael Broadbent successfully annexing both the 100 aad 220 Yards, and Willie Nankeville winning the Half-Mile event. Several members had competed in A.A.A. representative matches, the most successful perhaps being Len Herbert, who at the recent meeting at Portsmouth, clocked 9.32 for 2 miles, his own best figures, and the fastest 2 miles since the war. Owing to the curtailment of travelling only a meagre fixture list has been arranged for the coming winter season. The Polytechnic Harriers, both runners and walkers, have once again been invited to train from Belgrave Hall. Tribute was paid to Les Cohen (and his wife) for their zeal and successful handling of the Supporters' Club. Tribute was also paid to the untiring energy of Percy Wright in keeping the " Belgrave News Letter " right in front of all walking members. Whilst it was not policy to pick out and mention individual members by name, Syd Jarlett is an exception perhaps, as all those who have seen him with " his school " on the track, will agree. He has many fine youngsters under his wing and who will, we sincerely hope, bring succseses to the Club in the future. Our thanks are also due to Mrs. Churcher, Bill Brunning and Joe Wilson for so willingly providing prizes for the Track Walk on August 29th. To Joe Turner and Charlie Cook for their timekeeping; Mr. Fell as starter; Dick Savage for his "all the year round" assistance; George Still as junior pack trainer, and a host of others. Three new Vice-Presidents were elected, Alf. Harley, Jack Bidgood, and William Inge. In proposing Frank Webb as a Life Member, Harry Shields paid tribute to his untiring efforts both as a Track Captain and an athlete. In track matches particularly, Frank had at various times been called upon to perform at most events from 100 yards up to 10 miles, also all the recognised field events, and had helped score many valuable and needed points. The following were elected to the Committee:—E. Duffett, S. C. Roberts, L. Cohen, T. Morrell, T. Carter, T. C. Jones, G. Doubleday, R. J. Savage, H. Shields and A. E. Taylor. At a subsequent Committee Meeting, Bob. Readman was elected Walking Captain; Tom Carter as Running Captain, and Tom Cotton as Auditor.
